speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. On numerous occasions in this house questions have been asked of the government in respect to the proposed move of the T.C.A. repair facilities from Winnipeg to Montreal. The matter has been debated on various occasions in the house, and an important factor in the decision to move the repair base was a report submitted to the management of T.C.A. by a management consultant organization, Dixon-Speas.
On numerous occasions members of the house, as well as the government of the province of Manitoba, have asked that this report be made available to them so that the information and recommendations contained in it could be analysed and assessed. To date the government has refused to make this report available, either to members of the house or to the government of Manitoba; yet the Winnipeg Free Press of November 5 carried a report that the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz) wired the Prime Minister urging the appointment of a new person or tribunal to study the whole question.
The same news story reports that the Prime Minister replied that such an appointment would be an evasion of the government's responsibility and merely another delaying action, and the Prime Minister suggested that:
-the government of Manitoba and appropriate bodies in Winnipeg put forward all the evidence they could assemble on these other factors.
The same issue of the Winnipeg Free Press reports:
Mr. Pearson's telegram was read at the Winnipeg South Liberal association meeting Monday night. Mrs. Konantz said she had seen the Dixon-Speas report and could understand why it could not be made public. She said it contained information which could not be given to Canadian Pacific Air Lines, T.C.A.'s main competitor.
My point of privilege is that members of the house and the Manitoba government have been refused access to this important document upon which rests the main argument
for the movement of T.C.A. repair facilities from Winnipeg to Montreal, while the document has been shown to the hon. member for Winnipeg South. This demonstrates again partiality to government members and is an infringement of the rights of all other members of the House of Commons.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: In this connection, may I say that this appears to be another step toward contempt of parliament, and I should think the Prime Minister would be the one who would answer as to whether information was made available to the Liberal association of Winnipeg that has been denied to the parliament of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: I can deny that statement at once. Naturally I would be very glad to look into the report that has been given to the house from the press, and, either the Minister of Transport or I, if there is anything to be said on this matter, will say it in the house. Surely we cannot be expected to comment on a newspaper report of this importance without having had an opportunity to look into the matter. However, as far as the hon. gentleman's statement is concerned, I can deny it at once.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
I have to decide whether there is or is not a question of privilege. Once more I should like to refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 113, which reads in part as follows:
Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in

Question of Privilege
the debates or the proceedings of the house. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the house power to impose a reparation or apply a remedy.
I noticed that no motion followed the question of privilege. In the circumstances I must rule this is more in the nature of a criticism or a complaint than a question of privilege.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: May I say that I shall be glad, after I hear the statement by the minister explaining precisely what has happened in this matter, to move a motion tomorrow or whenever the minister may make his statement.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext: think it should be made clear this is not merely a complaint. The hon. member is raising a matter which is of vital concern to the privileges of this house, in that a document which has been denied to members of parliament and the government of Manitoba allegedly, according to the press, has been made available to a member of this house sitting on the government side. This is certainly a matter of privilege and not merely a complaint, if the hon. member's own statement is correctly reported. I think an explanation is due from the government as soon as they have an opportunity of interviewing that member and finding out whether she actually made the statement attributed to her.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. ORLIKOW  AVAILABILITY OF REPORT RESPECTING T.C.A. WINNIPEG MAINTENANCE BASE
speechtext:
As I said before, there is no doubt about the importance of the matter. However, if it is that important it should be followed by a motion. No motion was presented this morning. I do not mind taking the matter under consideration for a day or so. I think we will just leave it there, and I will take it under consideration and give a final decision tomorrow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time perhaps I might deal with the question asked on Friday by the Leader of the Opposition and that asked on Thursday by the hon. member for New Westminster with regard to the autobahn to Berlin.
I should say at once, of course, that we reject the implication in at least one of the questions with regard to the recent incident; it was suggested that the incident arose from provocative action on the part of the United States. On the contrary, the incident was the third in less than a month when the Soviet union has interfered with legitimate allied traffic.
There has, therefore, been no need on the part of Canada to make representations to the United States authorities. Throughout the recent incidents United States policy and resultant actions have been closely co-ordinated with the United Kingdom and France, who share primary responsibility concerning Berlin. We have been, of course, in close contact with the United States and our NATO allies who have acted in this matter, I believe, with care and restraint.
Although focused on what may seem to be minor points of procedure, incidents of this kind represent a continuing pressure by the Soviet union on the essential western right of free access to Berlin. They serve both as a reminder that this divided city remains a serious friction point in the improved east-west atmosphere and as a warning that the basic issues between east and west remain unsolved. Moreover, they reflect the ambivalent policy of the Soviet government, which on the one hand proclaims a policy of peaceful co-existence and, on the other, has recourse to military pressures in situations like those surrounding western rights of access to Berlin.
It is, of course, our view that all countries should seek to avoid provocative action particularly in delicate situations such as Berlin. We therefore hope that the Soviet union will ensure that their forces on the Berlin

Inquiries of the Ministry autobahn will cease to mar the improved atmosphere in east-west relations by such pressures, and will approach relations with the west in a manner which will be conducive to the conclusion of further and, we would hope, important agreements.
speakername: Hon. Paul  Marlin@Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
If you recall, Mr. Speaker, in 1957 the previous administration, under Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, had made agreements with the ten provinces respecting the fiscal relations which would exist for a five year period. The contracts were signed and these agreements were to be in existence for five years. A new government took office, a new government which had been expressing in opposition its concern over this constant tendency toward centralization of power in the federal government. This federal centralization was very noticeable in dominion-provincial relations, so it was only natural that there should be a statement of policy by the new government the minute this conference was called.
Let me emphasize again, Mr. Speaker, that there was no obligation on the new government of 1957 to call this conference. There were contracts in effect for five years which would have meant that we could have carried on without those tremendous increases in payments by the federal treasury to the provinces, which would have wiped out all the deficits we had during those five years. But in spite of the fact that there was an agreement with every province in Canada the new government called the provinces in, and in the opening paragraph of the report of the proceedings I have here appear the words of the then prime minister, Mr. Diefenbaker, the present Leader of the Opposition:
There have been times in the past when we have criticized the extent of federal participation in various common efforts on the part of the dominion and the provinces as inadequate. We have giver our undertaking that when new fiscal arrangements

are determined on, no province will receive less than it is now entitled to. But I want to make this clear at the beginning. We are not placing before you any "take it or leave it" attitudes; we are not taking any hard or fast positions. We are not placing before you any rigid formulae. This conference was convened to seek your ideas and your proposals. Clearly we cannot expect to solve all our major problems in two days, but we can hope in that time to have a general survey of many of them.
I quote that statement, Mr. Speaker, to demonstrate that from the very beginning of the Diefenbaker government there was an attitude that something had to be done about this relationship between the provinces and the federal government. Traditionally in Canada, like all federal states, there is a constant tug of war going on between the power of the provincial governments and that of the federal government. As conditions change the tendency is to swing one way and then another. Usually this tendency shows up in the federal house by the party in power tending to increase the position of the federal government and the party in opposition taking the opposite position to that taken by the party in power. This is normal and natural in the working out of democratic processes. For most of the early years of this period the federal government was represented by Conservatives. Naturally enough there was a strong movement to give power to the federal government as part of the effort to build up the country. The opposition to this growing strength came from a number of directions. The Liberal party defended the position of the provinces and became known in many areas as the provincial rights party. However, when the great emergency of the Hitler war arose the federal government gathered to itself tremendous powers, and used those powers in ways which were not always in keeping with tradition.
After the war was over this centralizing tendency continued and it was only natural that the opposition in those days should begin to express concern about this concentration of power in the hands of the federal government. It was understandable that when the Diefenbaker government took power we should have gone to the provinces, as the then Prime Minister did, and said to them "Let us have your ideas. They will be given consideration and then, after discussion, we shall arrive at a new fiscal arrangement".
Without going into detail about that arrangement, suffice it to say that the provinces were in fact granted a new deal. It cost the federal treasury a great deal of money. I might also say that in those discussions some of the provinces put forward demands which could only be described as extreme. Following the submissions and the discussions which
Lack of Consultation with Provinces took place some decision had to be made and, rightly or wrongly, it had to be made by the federal government at that time. However the offer of discussion was a step forward in this new concept which was evolving.
The next step had to do with my own department, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. It was the wish of the federal government to link the great resources of the north with the several areas of Canada to the south. We proposed to proceed with this undertaking, and we therefore suggested to the provinces a cooperative program of roads to resources. Roads are, of course, the prerogative of the provinces. Still, there is no use building a network of roads in the territories unless they are linked with the settled areas of the provinces.
The negotiations which took place in this connection lasted 14 months or more, because not a single agreement was signed with one province until every province had agreed to every clause and every comma. The type of discussion which went on was bilateral in character; we went through the long and arduous process of getting agreement in every province for agreement in every other province. Very soon we recognized that no government could carry out its propositions in such a way. No government could spend so much time on a single type of contract. The next step was to speed up the process.
The government decided to call a conservation conference. A decision to this effect was announced in Winnipeg on February 12, 1958, by the then prime minister. It was announced again in the house on August 30, 1958. In getting the plans ready it was clear once again that these renewable resources belonged, in most cases, to the provinces and were administered by the provinces. The federal government had joint responsibility in connection with fisheries and agriculture. So we had this situation; 10 provincial governments had the ownership and management of their own resources, while the federal government was responsible for ownership and management of the resources in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and the continental shelf off our shores.
In planning this conference the federal government took the lead in calling the ministers of all the provinces together. It said in effect "These resources are under your jurisdiction, but they will not amount to a great deal until we plan together for their best use; and their best use depends on trade policies, on monetary policies, on fiscal policies and, yes, even on taxation policies." We put this thesis before the 10 governments.

Lack of Consultation with Provinces They were governments of various political complexions. Two of them were Social Credit governments. One was a C.C.F. government. There were several Conservative governments. I have forgotten how many Liberal governments there were. But they all agreed as Canadians to work together for the better use of our resources. In this way there was cooperation in planning from beginning to end.
At the conclusion of that conference one of the recommendations was that the technique developed in the planning of those meetings should continue afterward in the management of our resources. So today we have for the first time in Canada's history a Canadian council of resource ministers. This council, representing 11 governments, is served by a secretariat which is bilingual, which does not owe loyalty to a province and which does not owe loyalty to the federal government; its loyalty is to the concept of the best possible development of our resources in Canada. This is the council which is receiving such favourable comments from newspapers across Canada. Let me read from the background paper put out by the Canadian council of resource ministers:
The Canadian council of resource ministers represents a new co-operative approach by the eleven senior governments of Canada to the many and varied problems in the field of resource development.
The council was founded on the basis of co-equal participation of the eleven senior governments and a rotating chairmanship. This operating formula has provided for the first time in Canadian history an intergovernmental forum within which resource policies are examined and co-ordinated.
It goes on to describe the organization of the council, pointing out that the present chairman is Hon. Rene Levesque from Quebec. Then it continues:
The Canadian council of resource ministers was established following the resources for tomorrow conference which took place in Montreal in October, 1961. The conference originated in an announcement by former prime minister John Diefenbaker on February 12, 1958, that a national conference on conservation would be called.
These are not my words; these are the words of the Canadian council of resource ministers.
The provincial premiers were invited to participate in preliminary discussions of the planning for such a conference. All provinces responded favourably, and the first meeting of the national steering committee, consisting of ministers from all provinces and the federal government was held November 17, 1958.
That is how far back precedent exists for this type of co-operation.
The conference reached a number of important conclusions. It found that lack of co-ordination between governments and between departments within governments had created a serious gap in resource development and management.
At the same time the conference recognized the existing system of Canadian federalism, in which

the ownership of natural resources largely rests with the provinces, while fiscal, monetary and trade policies are the responsibility of the federal government.
The senior governments subsequently agreed to the formation of a council. The council's formation was announced on February 6, 1962 following the final meeting of the resources for tomorrow steering committee.
At the same time an advisory committee was established to prepare for the first full meeting of the council in Toronto September 20-21, 1962.
I put those passages on record because they tell a story of accomplishment. They tell a story of what can be done when there is leadership, and patience in that leadership. They tell a story of how men of different political persuasions can sit down and work together as Canadians to achieve an end which will be of benefit for all Canadians. There was no hornet's nest stirring around the leadership of the government in those days in connection with resource development because we followed a type of co-operative federalism which took the tension out of the usual tug of war between the provinces and the federal government.

speechtext:
It has been suggested that I page Mr. Bennett. Let me tell the house that from 1944 to 1957 progress in discussions with the United States on the development of the Columbia river was almost exactly nil. There were 13 years of debating such silly subjects as only the record will show.
In 1957 and 1958 we laid the foundations for the treaty with the United States by two or three techniques. One of them was to set up a liaison committee between the federal government and the government of the province of British Columbia, with two ministers from each government on that committee. Every step that we took was agreed to by both cabinets, including the final draft of the treaty. Up until that time there was complete co-operation between the two governments.
I will not go into the reasons that caused the delay, but I will say that the present government know what the reasons are now that they are in power. All their talk in the house and throughout the country during the last two or three years that we were in power of how when they got into power they would solve the Columbia river problem just like that was nothing more than a fraud committed by a political party. Never question me about the Columbia river. If some of these people had put as much time and work on this matter as some others of us did they would know how hard we worked. When the record is placed before the committee which will consider this matter, many

members are going to get the surprise of their lives when they see the efforts made by the two governments, federal and provincial, to achieve co-operation and to make the project a success, because to go ahead with it would have been a matter of great pride to all Canadians.
I want to move on, Mr. Speaker. Sometimes the term "co-operative federalism" is not too well understood by provincial governments. Most of them refer to this approach as the ARDA approach because of the fact that the peculiar timing of events has made this phrase stick in their minds. If I may, I should like to go back in history a bit. In August, 1958 the then prime minister announced in the house a seven point national development program dealing primarily with agriculture. One of the points was a conservation policy, because the problems of agriculture could not be resolved purely within the realm of traditional agriculture alone.
It was our plan that the resources for tomorrow conference would be held in the fall of 1960. When the experts told the 11 governments that if it was held in the fall of 1960 they could not guarantee its success because their preparations were not complete I recall saying to the conference of ministers, as minister of agriculture at that time, that I would agree to the holding of the conference in 1961, a year later, to make sure it would not fail. However, I said that the needs of agriculture were such and our planning in the federal field in regard thereto had proceeded so far that we knew fairly well where we wanted to go, and as the federal minister I asked the steering committee to give me permission to go ahead and discuss with the provinces the subject of ARDA. We did not call it ARDA then; we just called it redevelopment.
They examined the situation. If you will go back and read the records of the House of Commons you will find that I gave my word that ARDA would in no way contravene the principles of the resources for tomorrow conference to be held that fall. The bill went through the house in the spring of 1961. Those provincial ministers accepted my word. We had established a condition of trust among us, and they accepted my word that ARDA would be co-ordinated with the efforts of the resource ministers council whose object was to bring together all departments of the federal and provincial governments in order to plan in the best interests of Canada. I honoured my commitments to the ministers on that council, and they honoured their word. They did not hinder me in any way in my efforts to get ARDA on the statute books before the resources for tomorrow conference was held.

As a matter of fact I saw all the agriculture ministers, first of all in conference here and then individually. Many members in the house will know that I visited those ministers. When I met the agriculture ministers I explained to them that the federal government wanted to achieve certain ends. I pointed out the necessity of moving in a certain way in connection with low income farmers across Canada. I said that before the federal government brought forward this legislation I should like to consult with each of the provinces individually and some of the provinces as a group.
It was during the ARDA discussions that the provinces first experienced this type of co-operative federalism, in that the then minister of agriculture or his officials discussed with them the planning of a new type of legislation that we wanted to bring before the house in Ottawa. I went to the extent of making speeches across the country advocating these principles. When I had secured the agreement of all the provinces for the type of thing we wanted to do I went to my colleagues in the cabinet and said "You asked me to prepare this legislation. I have consulted the provinces, and the legislation is the result of the co-operative efforts of all 11 ministers. There will be agreement all across the country".
The ARDA legislation was introduced into the house with the backing of all the provincial ministers and farm organizations. Even the opposition then did not oppose it. In fact there was so little opposition to the bill that I was forced to debate it on third reading myself in order to point out that there were some weaknesses in it. That shows you the extent to which you can get the provinces, farm organizations, business interests and political parties to work together if we put the needs of the country first and foremost. So the provinces refer to this co-operative federalism as the ARDA approach, and I am grateful for it; because it shows the complete harmony we had in introducing this legislation and carrying it out.
There is one thing more I should like to say in connection with ARDA, which I have already said but which I should like to emphasize. I guaranteed as a federal minister that nothing would be done under ARDA to contravene the principles that would be established by the resources for tomorrow conference. I kept my word. No minister throughout Canada, whether he is a minister of agriculture or a resources minister, will deny that, because they know I kept my word in so far as agriculture was concerned. Even though agriculture is one of the oldest and most strongly entrenched departments of the

Lack of Consultation with Provinces federal government, we always took our problems to the co-ordinating committee and cleared them with that committee. That was our intention, and all I can say at this time is that I hope this practice is still being carried out; because if you want to destroy something fine, if you want to destroy something good for Canada, just destroy the type of co-operation that we achieved in working out the ARDA program, and the type of program we achieved in working out the Canadian council of resource ministers.
I take some pride in telling this story. I hope it will be told all across Canada. I think our actions created a new concept of co-operative federalism compared with the former situation. Where federalism used to be a tug of war we tried to establish a basis on which we could work co-operatively in those fields where there is joint jurisdiction, in those fields where the provinces wanted us to work with them or we wanted them to work with us.
But it was not only in the department I headed that this course was followed. Sitting beside me in the house today is the former minister of labour. I recall where the idea came from for the winter works incentive program. I recall the tremendous efforts he made as minister of labour to consult not only with all the provinces but right down to the municipal level before introducing this program. He always considered their wishes with regard to this matter as having priority.
Here you had in the Department of Labour under the Diefenbaker government the same type of approach by way of co-operative federalism that I have demonstrated was the case in the resource field, and particularly with regard to agriculture. Furthermore, when I went to the then minister of labour with the story of how there were great problems in education in the rural areas of Canada it was he who took the initiative in the field of education by calling the provincial ministers together with their staffs. We had a great backlog of uneducated Canadians with less than the normal opportunity to obtain an education. What kind of curriculum could you set up to give these many thousands of Canadians the opportunity they deserved? There was no resentment on the part of the ministers of education and their staffs. We simply put forward the need, and the governments of the provinces, representing every national political party, co-operated. But the leadership came from the minister at the federal level. He knew he had no rights with regard to education from the point of view of jurisdiction, but Canadians had a need so far as this particular aspect of education was concerned. Naturally I worked through the minister of labour. I tell you these things because this philosophy was pervading all departments.
[Mr. Hamilton.!
I also recall the efforts made by the former minister of national health and welfare in talking to the provinces and holding long consultations with them before he did anything. So far as hospitals are concerned he went right down to the hospital organizations and medical associations. There was always consultation ahead of time. His efforts were always directed to trying to achieve the maximum support for various ideas that would help the whole of Canada. Yet surely health is the prerogative of the provincial governments.
This concept of federal-provincial co-operation extends into many fields. This is the place for a federal co-operative system, and this is the place for accepting the lessons we have learned over the last five or six years.

The forest industry is the most important one we have in Canada. Once again the forests are owned and managed by the provinces, but the federal government has to give leadership because it has a tremendous influence on forestry through trade, fiscal and monetary policies, and through taxation.
If we sit back and say we are going to get out of this field and let the provinces go it alone, we will go back to the type of situation they had in the United States before 1787; 13 separate, sovereign states with a little government up on top that had no power and was useless. Canada is our country. We were second in the world in pioneering

the federal concept. We think that in this new dimension we have added to federalism we have added a dimension that equals the original concept of confederation as pronounced at the 1787 convention of Philadelphia. When the house took recess I was on the point of moving an amendment to the motion that you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker. I read the amendment into the record so that all parties would have an idea what it was. I should like to sum up what I was saying this morning by listing the indictment I tried to make.
We condemn the leadership of the present government on the grounds of its behaviour and action in connection with the municipal loan and development fund. We condemn it for its failure to act with regard to the Canada pension plan. We condemn it for its attitude in connection with the Department of Industry, not only because of its decision to designate areas without consulting the municipalities concerned but also because of the serious overlapping which occurs with the powers and activities of municipalities.
We condemn the present government and its leadership for the method used in announcing its withdrawal from the joint programs. We know this intention was originally announced in the course of a speech at a nominating convention in Quebec city two elections ago when the President of the Privy Council was nominated. That speech was made by the present Prime Minister, who was then leader of the opposition. We have since heard the President of the Privy Council repeat this speech at a meeting in Toronto and go into great detail with regard to the proposal. This has caused serious disturbance in the minds of members of provincial governments across this country. Possibly it is because the President of the Privy Council has a reputation in Quebec as a centralist that he was forced to make the statement he did in order, if possible, to prove he was not a centralist. However, by making this speech he has encouraged even more extreme statements to be made by people who would ordinarily have awaited developments before reaching conclusions.
The way this statement was made is another example of confusion and bumbling by the present government in making announcements which seriously affect agreements between the federal government and the provinces. Tremendous confusion has been caused by this approach. I could mention many examples, but I should like to remind the house of what was said in connection with university scholarships. Just after the present Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources took office he went out to the west coast and announced that a far reaching scheme would be set up immediately. This aroused great expectations. As

far as we can gather the provinces were never consulted about this scheme. Well, an announcement was made and nothing happened. I am simply saying it looks as though there is another retreat in this area, too. The minister says something is going to be done, but there is no action. Therefore we must assume the government has retreated. Once again they have gone into a provincial sphere and talked about what they were going to do. There is no evidence that any province was consulted, and now we find no evidence of action.
I notice that the Minister of Agriculture is not here, but I wonder if he has ever called together the eastern advisory committee of the Canadian wheat board. There is a serious problem facing the eastern part of Canada, the maritime provinces, in connection with grain. We have here a board representative of the provinces concerned which when occasion demands, meets with the government agency, the Canadian wheat board, to help resolve difficulties of this kind. There is no evidence that the present government is making any use of the consultation machinery which was provided by the previous government as a means of supplying answers to these problems.
But the most damning indictment of all, especially in the mind of the public, is based on the course of events with regard to the Canada pension plan. Here we had a plain statement of the government's intention, the central plank of the election campaign. Yet because of a waspish and witch-like attack on the premier of a province, the whole matter has become embroiled in side issues. The government has had to retreat and, once again, the general wishes of the provinces are not consulted.
However, there are some signs that certain members of the government are aware of the need for co-operation. For example, the Minister of Forestry, in the statement he made on his estimates, did indicate his awareness that he could get good ideas from the provinces and that more rapid progress could be achieved in this field by working in co-operation with the provinces.
On the other hand the Minister of Fisheries does not seem so convinced. I have been watching for some sign of leadership from the central government so the great knowledge and experience which has been built up federally can be used to do something of benefit for the fishing industry in cooperation with the premiers of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Quebec as part of a joint program. A great need exists, yet there is little evidence of such leadership coming forward. The only leadership of which I

This type of development could give Canadian federalism new life, new hope, new fellowship, and new effectiveness. It will open up the prospect of a future of co-operation instead of conflict. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, on behalf of the official opposition, has moved a no confidence motion condemning the government for its failure to carry out the spirit of co-operative federalism and for neglecting to consult with the provinces before announcing or undertaking programs which fall wholly or partly within provincial jurisdiction.
