maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
However, the hon. member has raised what is a crucial question for parliament and for the people of Canada, and I think he has performed a great service in raising this matter. Sir John A. Macdonald once said Canada was a difficult country to govern. Again and again throughout our history there have been times when it appeared that Canadian confederation was going to disintegrate, but always the good sense of the Canadian people has rallied and we have managed to resolve our difficulties and go on as a united people.
I am convinced that in this present critical situation the good sense of the Canadian people will once again assert itself. I believe we will meet the difficulties which now confront us, but it will only be done if we are prepared to look carefully at our problems, be as non-partisan as possible in seeking solutions, and endeavour to get a spirit of unity in working out the problems of confederation.
One of the difficulties is that we are confusing two questions. We are confusing the matter of biculturalism and the matter of federal-provincial fiscal relations. I think we have to separate them in our thinking. We must first of all accept the spirit of co-operative federalism, and by that we in this party mean that the two founding races, the French speaking and English speaking races, came together in a pact which we call the British North America Act. That constitution guaranteed to the French speaking people of Canada certain basic rights; and there is a feeling in the province of Quebec today, which I personally think is justified in some respects, that English speaking Canada has not always lived up to the spirit of confederation. Whether we agree with that statement or not, the fact remains that even if people feel they have a grievance then there is a problem, and I think all Canadians have to stop and accept the fact that in French Canada today there is a sense of grievance. There is a feeling that they have not been allowed to play their full part within the spirit of Canadian confederation, and this is something which has to be faced up to honestly, patiently, and with understanding.
The present government recognized this when it set up the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. I am sure all of us hope that as a result of the representations which are made to that body we will get a report that will chart a course for the future, that will bring the two races together in a spirit of harmony within the Canadian confederation.
Of course this situation is not helped by the extremists on the one hand who talk about taking Quebec out of confederation, who use the most violent terms associated with
Lack of Consultation with Provinces separatism; nor is it helped on the other hand by statements such as those contained in yesterday's Globe and Mail, reporting a speech made by the premier of British Columbia, which says:
B.C. will not even listen let alone agree to any basic changes in the British North America Act at the interprovincial conference in Ottawa this month, Premier W. A. C. Bennett said Saturday night-
Mr. Bennett indicated that Quebec cannot expect British Columbia to support its demands for a special place for the French language and culture in Canada.
"Federal civil servants should be appointed on merit and merit alone," he said. "We will not stand for civil servants getting more money for talking two languages, or three languages for that matter."
If anything is needed in Canada today it is for people, particularly leaders in positions of responsibility, to approach this problem with an open mind and an understanding heart.
But, Mr. Speaker, there are much deeper problems which should not be confused with the question of biculturalism, and they are problems that have beset confederation ever since 1867. A federal system is always difficult to administer, and the Canadian federal system has been no exception. The Rowell-Sirois commission was set up in the late 1930's because parliament and the government of that day recognized there were three problems facing the federal and provincial governments. The first was that since confederation the responsibilities which had been allocated to the provinces under the British North America Act have grown and expanded, without any increase in the sources of revenue with which the provinces might discharge these increased responsibilities.
In 1867 giving to the provinces responsibility for education, welfare, health and resource development did not involve large sums of money. In those days there were no such things as unemployment insurance, old age pensions or widows' pensions, and no one thought of health services as much more than elementary sanitary services. Consequently the provinces were not allocated fields of revenue that could meet expanded services in education, health, welfare and resource development.
With the passing of the years, with the growing pressure of public opinion for better education, better health services, expanded pensions and more adequate resource development, the provinces found they were not in a financial position to discharge the responsibilities allocated to them by the constitution. The people of Canada saw new programs surging ahead in other nations. They saw universal pensions, unemployment insurance and health services being introduced in Great Britain and the Scandinavian countries, and

Lack of Consultation with Provinces they demanded that something of this sort be done in Canada. The provinces since then have been finding it increasingly difficult to do these things on the very limited tax revenues which have been allocated to them.
The second problem which has been bedevilling confederation is that the federal government, viewing the whole national picture, has been increasingly aware of the fact that there has been a lack of uniformity in the minimum standards of education, health and welfare enjoyed by people in different parts of Canada. Now, it is not the concern of one province to worry about the standards of another province, but it is a responsibility of the federal government to recognize that a Canadian citizen has a right to the same minimum standards of education, health and welfare whether he lives in Prince Edward Island, in the province of Manitoba or the province of British Columbia. Therefore the whole question of equalization has been to the fore.
The third problem that has faced confederation is the lack of capital resources to develop the natural resources of the respective provinces. Some of the provinces have the capital, or nearly enough capital, to develop their resources, but many of the provinces in Canada cannot and will not be able to develop their resources unless there is some equalization of capital allocation.
What have we done about these three problems? The Rowell-Sirois commission made certain recommendations. Hon. members will remember that those recommendations were scuttled by the premiers of two provinces. During the war there were temporary tax rental agreements. After the war Right Hon. Mackenzie King called a federal-provincial conference on reconstruction with a view to returning to the problem that the Rowell-Sirois commission had examined and had sought to solve. Out of that conference we began to move toward a solution of the three problems which the Rowell-Sirois commission had put forth in such clear and succinct terms. We tried to meet the problem of the provinces having inadequate tax revenues with which to discharge their constitutional responsibilities by entering into tax rental agreements. Surely nobody in Canada ever wants to go back to the tax jungle that existed prior to the tax rental agreements coming into effect. This is one thing to which the parliaments of Canada and the provinces should adhere.
The other thing that has developed has been equalization grants to reduce the disparity in income as between various provinces in Canada. When I hear some individuals

making speeches about the fact that the province of Quebec could manage its own financial affairs if only the federal government would stay out of certain tax fields and leave these matters to them, I think those persons ought to remember that the province of Quebec receives a larger share of the equalization grants than any other province in Canada. If I remember correctly it is some $69 million a year. They are entitled to it; I am glad they get it, but it should be remembered that Quebec is one of the provinces whose average per capita income falls below the national average, and the province of Quebec has as much of an incentive as any other province in Canada to continue tax rental agreements and tax equalization.
The other way in which this problem of provincial revenue has been overcome has been by means of shared programs. I submit that these shared programs have been of great value, and I think many of them ought to be retained. Also we have had conditional grants under which the federal government has made certain moneys available to the provinces providing they spend them for certain purposes and in certain ways. I will have something to say about the question of conditional grants later on. We have sought to establish some equalization across Canada by means of giving the provinces a share of the taxes which can be used for education. I believe that one of the best ways we could help the provinces which are going to be under increasing pressure for better educational services is not for the federal government to get into the field of education, which will only arouse antagonism in certain parts of Canada, but rather to give to the provinces a larger portion of the shared tax fields in order that they can use this money to lift some of the school tax burden off their municipalities.
We have helped establish better social services by means of pensions, family allowances and shared programs. Hospital insurance has been another means of equalizing the burden of providing social services in Canada, and some assistance has been given to the provinces for resource development. So we have begun in Canada to find some solution to the problems that beset federal-provincial relations.
But while we want to do everything we can to enable the provinces to have sufficient financial resources of their own in order that they may discharge their responsibilities, and while we want to have a minimum of interference in provincial jurisdiction, I suggest to those who talk about provincial rights that they must give equal consideration to leaving the federal government the

power to discharge its responsibilities. It the federal government is weakened in its fiscal capacity to meet the problems of economic stagnation and unemployment, then we will be in a bad position in Canada. No provincial premier will say that he is responsible for unemployment in his province and is prepared to take the burden off the federal government. Every provincial premier, and rightly so, says unemployment is primarily a federal matter. But if the federal government is to assume responsibility for promoting economic growth and providing full employment, it must have the fiscal means at its disposal to put money into circulation in times of deflation and to contract the amount of money in circulation in times of inflation. It must be able to-

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: It is monetary.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it is monetary. It is more than monetary. Monetary policy has to do with issuing the money, but fiscal policy has to do with distributing it; that is, so it can raise taxes and take money out of circulation, and ease taxes to put more money into circulation when necessary by providing housing, and so on; so it can have a shelf of public works, federal and provincial, by which money can quickly be put into circulation to create employment.
In my opinion no prime minister in Canada has a mandate from the Canadian people to preside over the dissolution of confederation. My plea to the Prime Minister is that, while approaching this problem of federal-provincial relations and doing everything possible to help the provinces meet some of the problems which I have just outlined, he should not weaken Canada in its capacity to deal with the great major problems of economic growth and full employment in this country. I cannot do better than quote the words which Right Hon. Mackenzie King used when he was opening the federal-provincial conference on reconstruction in 1945. They are worth remembering. He said:
The lessons of war have taught us the vital importance of co-operation in an effort to reach a common goal. Without unity there is frustration. Now that we are coming face to face with the problems of the post-war years, the need for unity and co-operation is not less than it has been: from some points of view, it is greater. The enemies we shall have to overcome will be on our own Canadian soil. They will make their presence known in the guise of sickness, unemployment and want. It is to plan for a unified campaign in Canada against these enemies of progress and human wellbeing that we have come together at this time.
I suggest that these enemies of sickness, unemployment and want are still present in our society, and that the federal government must retain the fiscal powers necessary to cope with them. I suggest that we need power
Lack of Consultation with Provinces to deal effectively with the economic fluctuations. We need the power to forestall economic stagnation and unemployment. The federal government needs the necessary power to provide the equalization of services as between the various areas of Canada. When some provinces say "We can go it alone", it seems to me that this is a very narrow and parochial outlook.
It is true that a provincial government has to think primarily in terms of its own citizens, but we in this parliament and the government have to think in terms of all the people of Canada. Nothing would do more to wreck confederation than to balkanize Canada, to give up fiscal powers that would result in one part of Canada enjoying prosperity while the other parts of Canada lived on a level of income that bordered on degradation. Part of the responsibility of the federal government and the federal parliament is to see to it that there is a distribution of income among the various areas of Canada so that a Canadian citizen, whether he comes from the middle of Canada, the Pacific coast or the Atlantic coast, is guaranteed a certain minimum standard of living, and has the right to a job and to a decent measure of economic security.
The federal government must, in my opinion, retain sufficient revenue so it can provide capital investment for resource development, particularly in the underdeveloped areas of Canada. We hear a great deal these days about helping the underdeveloped areas of the world. There is no party, Mr. Speaker, more interested in that or more anxious for Canada to do its part in that regard than this party. But charity begins at home. We all recognize that in Canada there are provinces with vast resources which cannot be developed unless they get some assistance in terms of capital investment.
I agree that the federal government should proceed with preparations for the Canada pension plan. There has been some criticism that the provinces have not been consulted. I agree that they should be consulted. But I maintain also that the present government made a commitment to the Canadian people to provide a contributory, universal portable pension plan, and that the Canadian people took that commitment at face value. This government has a responsibility to put that plan on the statute books, after consultation with the provinces; and no province should be allowed to stop the Canadian government from doing what it promised the Canadian people it would do.
There has been some criticism of the fact that the government did not consult the

Lack of Consultation with Provinces provinces about the municipal loan and development fund. I think that was regrettable. However, after they did consult the provinces the provinces recommended certain changes which were accepted and put into effect. This plan is in operation. I think instead of criticizing the government for the municipal loan and development fund legislation, we might do well to remember that the provincial governments and the mayors and municipalities of this country, have been pleading with successive governments for 18 years to put that kind of legislation on the statute books. It was long overdue.
I would say the same thing is true with reference to the Canada development fund. The Canada development corporation is something which is badly needed to stimulate economic growth in the underdeveloped parts of Canada, particularly to supply the kind of capital that the provinces cannot possibly supply to promote economic growth in their areas and to provide jobs for their people. Again, I think where the provinces are involved there should be consultation, but that consultation does not give the federal government any excuse for failure to proceed as expeditiously as possible to put that plan into effect.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit one question?

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: Having said what he has said, does the hon. member feel then that the Liberal government should have consulted the provinces before they made the promise on the universal pension plan, instead of before they introduced the legislation?

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
No, I do not feel they should have consulted the provinces before they made the promise. I think the responsibility of any federal party going before the Canadian people is to map out what is constitutionally possible, to decide what their program is, and then consult the people of Canada. Then the responsibility is not to get cold feet when they meet opposition, but to carry out the commitments they have made to the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has moved this motion of no confidence in the government because of its failure to carry out the spirit of co-operative federalism and for neglecting to consult with the provinces. I want to say, in the first place, that I doubt very much if the Conservative party can pat itself on the back to any extent for either its development of the spirit of co-operative federalism or for its consultation with the provinces. If we are in a mess today, then both the previous Conservative and Liberal governments contributed to it. When I was

listening to the exchange of religious pleasantries by the Secretary of State who said "Alleluia"-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: I deny that, sir.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
I exonerate the Secretary of State. One of the Liberal members said "Alleluia" and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said "Amen". I was going to suggest that they both ought to come to the penitents bench when we are looking at the mess in which Canada is at the moment. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the time has come to stop blaming each other. I do not believe the people of Canada care very much whether it was the Conservatives or the Liberals who made things worse than they were. As a matter of fact I am not as pessimistic as some speakers. I am not as pessimistic as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who says that the federal-provincial conference later this month is likely to be a dismal failure. I think we have made some progress.
I attended the conference in 1945 called by Mr. Mackenzie King, the federal-provincial conference on reconstruction. We have come a long way in the 18 years that have intervened, and both Liberal and Conservative governments have contributed in some measure to the progress we have made. We have not made nearly enough progress. We are in a critical situation now, but it will not help to solve the problems if we spend time trying to allocate blame. What we have to do is recognize that this country faces a crisis in federal-provincial relations.
We have faced such crises before, and our forefathers met them successfully. I believe we can meet these crises which are now upon us, both that concerning biculturalism and that which has to do with fiscal relations as between the government of Canada and the respective provinces. But if we are to do that we will have to approach this problem not as citizens of a single province but as citizens of Canada. We will have to start with the assumption that Canada must continue as a great nation; that the government of that nation must have the necessary powers to act like the government of a great nation; that the provinces have problems, and that they must be helped to solve those problems. But it will not help the provinces to solve their problems if we denude the federal government of the fiscal authority it needs to lead this country along the road toward prosperity and economic well-being.
I am going to propose an amendment, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is hardly fitting to criticize the government, or to go further and condemn the government, for its failure to carry out the spirit of co-operative

federalism when this government has been less than seven months in office.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: Look at the mess.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
My hon. friend says look at the mess. I can assure him the mess was not all made during the last seven months. I think what we have to do instead is to urge the government to be more aggressive than it now is in tackling this problem; that we must say to the government "We expect you to implement more fully the spirit of co-operative federalism. We expect you to co-operate with the provinces. Above all, we expect you to give this country the kind of leadership it needs in the present world situation". Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Port Arthur:
That the amendment be amended, (a) by deleting the words "condemns the government for its failure to carry out" and by substituting therefor the words "urges the government to carry out more fully"; (b) by deleting the words "for its neglect"; and (c) by deleting the words "wholly or partly" and by substituting the words "to any extent", so that the amendment as amended would then read;
"That this house urges the government to carry out more fully the spirit of co-operative federalism and to consult with the provinces before announcing or undertaking programs which fall to any extent within provincial jurisdiction".
In moving the amendment we are not saying we are satisfied with the way in which the government has conducted federal-provincial relations. The government has only been in office a short time, but we would urge them to be more vigorous and aggressive; and if they are we can assure them they will have the support of the great majority of Canada's citizens.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that while the extremists on both sides are most vociferous, I believe the great majority of the Canadian people want to retain Canada as a nation; they want a government at Ottawa with the power which will enable the country to act like a nation and conduct itself like a nation. If we are to find the answer to the problems of federal-provincial relations we shall do so only if we come to them in a spirit of unity and also in a spirit of sympathy and understanding. Unless we are prepared to see that many of the grievances which have arisen need rectification, unless we are prepared to see each other's point of view, this crisis will grow worse. But if we are prepared to approach each problem in a spirit of sympathy and mutual understanding, then I am convinced that this parliament and this government, if it aggressively tackles the problem, can do much to establish in Canada a spirit of unity.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to express
Lack of Consultation with Provinces my gratitude to the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle for bringing up this topic which he has introduced this afternoon. I am convinced that it is one of the most urgent and vital problems with which we should be concerning ourselves in this house, because as the previous speaker has just mentioned certainly our nation stands at a critical time in its history.
There is a saying "Marry in haste, repent at leisure". In this regard I agree with the mover of the amendment in condemning certain programs to which the government has hastily become wedded. Such would include the municipal development and loan fund, some of the budget resolutions, the Canada pension plan, and there are others. However, in fairness to the government I believe I should say that it has shown quite an unusual capacity for repentance. It repented a little in regard to the budget; it reached a compromise with the provinces in relation to the municipal development and loan fund. Two weeks from now the subject of the Canada pension plan will be raised at a meeting of the federal government with the provincial premiers. I sincerely hope this will provide the opportunity for a little more repentance.
As leader of a minority party and as a member of the opposition in this house, my choice in these debates is at best that of the lesser of two evils. This not only applies to many of the arguments which have been brought up by the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle concerning his charge against the government; it also relates to the record that his own government set in the previous administration, and I think as it relates to this particular subject with which we are concerned this afternoon it certainly concerns the government that that party followed as well.
In the twenty fifth parliament the government appeared not to do very much at all, and because nothing was done to solve the problems we are thinking about, not many mistakes were made. In the present parliament, in many instances which could be mentioned, the government has rushed in where the angels of the previous government feared to tread. Some of the policies introduced were obviously ill advised. On the other hand, the government's surprising capacity for having second thoughts and taking a second look has saved us from any actual disaster.
We have heard a lot today about co-operative federalism. Accepting the premise that we do face a great number of problems in Canada which concern the provinces, as well as the federal government, which concern the
4632	HOUSE OF
Lack of Consultation with Provinces whole nation, as well as the question of Canada being a nation at all, I think that what we need at this moment is a little bit of co-operative parliamentarianism. I believe we could solve some of our difficulties more effectively if we showed more of this spirit than our record in the past several months has indicated us capable of doing. I say this particularly in light of the fact that for the second time in as many years we find ourselves in a situation in this house where the government does not command an absolute majority.
In these circumstances I certainly believe it would not be in the best interests of the country if the government were overthrown on the basis of the proposition which has been advanced this afternoon. For one thing, we would be denying the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the chance of hearing directly from the provincial premiers what they feel the government should be doing in the field of federal-provincial relations. We would also be denying him a further chance to repent with regard to certain measures which, I believe, have been brought in too hastily without adequate consultation with the provinces.
We heard a good deal about co-operative federalism in the speech from the throne. I imagine this is a phrase which has been left without an owner since the days when the old co-operative commonwealth federation became the New Democratic party. I imagine that both the old line parties, seeing a policy of such shiny appearance and high sounding name lying around unclaimed, have hastily grasped it to add it to their bag of tricks. Like the expression biculturalism, it is one of those expressions which are easy enough to use but far less easy to define. Nevertheless, if what it means is an exchange of ideas between the provinces and the federal government before they are put into effect, I am all for it. Indeed, this is why, according to my understanding, the forthcoming provincial premiers conference has been called.
The former minister of agriculture called attention to an important matter when he spoke of the need for more co-operation at the government level especially with regard to the development of our natural resources. His comments apply particularly to the ARDA program to which he referred in the course of his remarks. He spoke about the spirit of ARDA. But as I look back on the history of that project, all that I recall the federal government saying at that time was that they were willing to invest some federal funds in this project for the rehabilitation of agriculture across the country, while the real work was done by the ministries of agriculture in the different provinces. That is probably not wrong; and is as it should be. But what was


needed in those days, as it is needed now, is the motivation and the desire, as well as the necessary mechanics, to make sure that consultation to these ends should take place at both levels and at the time it is called for.
Mention might be made of the whole program of vocational training. We have a number of fine institutions built with the taxpayers' money across this country. We have one such institution in my home city and I am sure many other hon. members have similar institutions in their own communities. Here again, there was a woeful lack of consultation before this program was put into operation. Its result is only too apparent. In many instances building construction was completed far in advance of the actual need. In others, buildings were located in places where it was impossible to give maximum effectiveness to the program. This emphasizes once again how important it is to make sure that when the federal government brings forward any proposals or any legislation which overlaps certain functions of the provincial governments, such proposals should be carried out only after there has been the necessary consultation.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle was perfectly right to point out that businessmen and even politicians could work together when they put the interest of their country first. I am confident, as I have said before, that no one individual, or no one group in this house, has all the answers to the problems which we face today. If we expect co-operative federalism to mean anything, then it is time we demonstrated a spirit of co-operative parliamentarianism in our work here as well. We can do with plenty of this co-operative spirit in the house. I share the enthusiasm the hon. member for Qu'Appelle displayed about the way we do things out west. I believe the two Social Credit governments in the west are an example to us, particularly with regard to resource development in the interest of their people. Looking across this nation I believe any prime minister would be hard put to develop on the national scene a government which could equal the efficiency and the standard set by most of the provincial governments in Canada at the present time.
This brings us again to the problem we confront in making Canada a nation. All too often, our provincial loyalties and our sectional interests are more firmly based than our national concern. Here again, if we are to make confederation work, it is essential we should begin at the national level so that the impact of what we are doing may spread to the provinces. Already many of the provinces are ahead of us. When we look at the machinery which exists to provide for cooperation between the federal government

and the provinces, machinery which the present government inherited from the previous Conservative government and which they, in turn, inherited from the previous Liberal government, we find it is pitifully inadequate.
Perhaps it is because of the commission on biculturalism and bilingualism which has just begun its work; perhaps it is because there is so much talk in our country now about whether we are to survive as a nation, that I am concerned about interpreting afresh what was in the minds of the original fathers of confederation when they brought into being the Dominion of Canada, to which has been added the succession of provincial divisions since 1867. As I study these early debates and the proceedings of the Quebec conferences which were beginning to take form about 100 years ago today, I find there were two basic principles involved. First, there was a determination to make one nation of this country despite all odds and discouragement. We might say that there was a negative motivation then, because there was a strong desire that this part of North America should not simply fall into the hands of the United States. But whatever the underlying purposes were, these men faced tremendous decisions and tremendous problems which in my view were greater in their day than those we face now. But they did so and they succeeded because there was a determination to make sure that a nation, Canada, came into being and that it did so on such a basis that it could survive.
Second, there was the determination that in making this nation the freedom of every individual would be preserved, that every inhabitant would have the right to preserve his traditional way of life and that in so far as possible these rights would be preserved by law and constitutional safeguards. This did not just apply to the individual. It also applied to the individual provinces concerned. This is why when we go back and study the terms of the act which gave us this country, Canada, we find there were certain definite safeguards outlined and that the authority of the provinces and the authority of the federal government were defined. I maintain that if there were a little greater concern and determination on our part today to make sure that Canada remains a nation and if there were just a little more determination and clearcut thinking on how we can safeguard the rights of the provinces and at the same time give ourselves a federal government that would project itself into a continuing nation, we would not have all the problems we face now.
The second principle of protecting individual rights and provincial rights is in direct contrast to the melting pot theory that
Lack of Consultation with Provinces has been so common and so dominant in the political development of the United States. It was the basis of confederation and is the very essence of Canadianism today. I believe it is to these two guiding principles that we refer when we talk about the spirit of confederation, that very spirit which is at the heart of Canada itself. If we can face our present problems unitedly in the same spirit of purpose and in the same spirit of intent, then Canada and Canadians can look forward to the future with more enthusiasm and more optimism than is the case at the present time.
The instrument that was designed to carry out these purposes was the statute passed by the United Kingdom parliament that we know as the British North America Act. This act constituted the original provinces into a new nation, Canada. Most significantly, it abandoned the original idea of a single unified government consisting predominantly of French Canadian Lower Canada and Anglo-Saxon Upper Canada and divided them into the two provinces which are our largest provinces today, the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. It reserved matters of legislation for the federal government, and this was essential if Canada was to become a nation. But it also reserved certain subjects of legislation for the provinces, generally those of a local nature as we can see if we study the document. It gave the assurance that the individual rights of the provinces and of the people who live in those provinces would be safeguarded. It embodied certain guarantees of religious liberty and freedom in education and, whether intentionally or not, it made sure that these techniques would be made effective by requiring that no constitutional amendment could be made without action first by the United Kingdom parliament.
Undoubtedly, however, the development of Canada has in some ways not taken place as our founders intended that it should. This is the reason for the discussion we have today relating to the co-operation and the working together of the provincial governments and the federal government here in Ottawa. As I have already mentioned, I believe that the provinces in many ways and in spite of their difficulties have done a better job than has been done at the federal level. Many Canadians, and this does not apply only to the people of Quebec, have a loyalty to their own province, their own people and their own characteristic ways of life that runs more deeply than their loyalty to Canada as a nation. This is understandable and it is not a basically undesirable thing.
But this does bring us to the point that in one area we have fallen short of the original intention of the founding fathers, to

Lack of Consultation with Provinces make Canada a nation. In too many cases there has been a complete lack of continuous liaison between the federal and provincial governments. In some areas, indeed, the provinces have been forced, through lack of federal action in a field, to assume powers that originally were contemplated to belong to the federal authorities. We have come a long way from the intention of our founding fathers that, come what may, we would make a nation.
In the last two election compaigns the Social Credit party has insisted that the federal government should take a more realistic approach to the problem of liaison with the provinces. We have talked about it continually in the house. During the private members' hour in the last parliament it was my privilege to present a proposition based on this very same thing. We intend to do the same again in this parliament. The proposition is simply that it is time that the federal government established, not just a secretariat but a full and complete department with a cabinet minister in charge of it which might be called the ministry of federal-provincial affairs. This ministry would be charged with the responsibility of working out those matters which relate to both levels of government.
In reading the agenda of the forthcoming conference with the provincial premiers on November 25 I am very pleased to find that under item 5 there will be a discussion of continuing federal-provincial liaison arrangements. I would urge the Prime Minister at this time to seize this opportunity to discuss with the provincial premiers their opinions with regard to setting up such a department at the federal level. This is not a new idea. It is something that a great number of men concerned with provincial governments are talking about now, and already several of the provinces have taken the lead and have set up their own departments of provincial-federal affairs. I mention this now because I think this is an excellent and opportune time for definite discussions to take place towards this end.
This country is in urgent need of development on a national basis from the point of view of national programs. We need a national highways program. We will never have a system of national highways if we look at the matter only from the point of view of sectional interest alone. The use of our water resources is also a very important matter. The problem of water pollution is something that concerns the nation as a whole, and measures cannot be planned effectively except on an interprovincial basis. There is the question of a national electric grid, which is something that at the present time requires

more action and less talk. There is the matter of federal-provincial financial arrangements which is highlighted by the request of Premier Lesage of Quebec. Many of the points Premier Lesage is asking for, as he seeks to meet the fiscal needs within his own province, are the very items that were guaranteed in the original confederating arrangement. They are things which more than just one province is thinking about and talking about today.
We have heard some discussion this afternoon relating to the various cost sharing programs; but why, and under what definition of administrative efficiency can we expect, or should we expect the federal government to be collecting taxes, which in turn it hands back to the provinces? In order to hand them out, it has to retain a certain amount of control. Why should not the federal government step out completely from some of its tax collecting fields and give the provinces the responsibility?
If I understand correctly what I read in the papers and hear from different politicians at the provincial level, the whole question of hospital insurance is in desperate trouble at the present time. We will need a federal-provincial conference to talk about this before too long. There is also the question of the federal government's responsibility in the field of health. Mr. Speaker, it is not good enough that we continue as we have been going on.
Not to belabour the point, or take too much time in the discussion this afternoon, I would only say that if the federal government is not to become hopelessly bogged down in the future, in introducing programs here and withdrawing them there, making enemies of the provincial governments more through clumsiness than through conflicts of policy, such a ministry or department of government is urgently required. Such a department could provide the channels of organization and communication, backed by the authority of a minister of the crown. It would on a permanent basis be able to discuss with the provincial governments the impact of the different levels of government on each other.
This proposition is not something new. In the United States, which has a federal government set-up, there is a secretary of the interior whose basic responsibility is the very thing I am talking about. In the commonwealth of Australia, where the autonomous rights of the states are even more clearly defined than some of the rights of our provinces, it has moved forward to take such action.
I would respectfully urge the Prime Minister to consider this, and consider it in

the immediate future. We should not be dragging the provincial premiers to Ottawa every three or four months, each time a problem comes up on which their advice is needed. This is the type of crisis government which has been too typical of our federal administration for too long. Why cannot we see into the future and anticipate some of these problems before we come to them? That is why the consultative aspect of government, particularly on the federal government level, is something which is most urgent.
My sincere hope is that this coming federal-provincial conference will be the starting point for some permanent means by which provincial consultation in all fields can take place. Somehow I wish yesterday had not been a holiday. Our debating time on this important subject is limited now because the debate on the supply motion closes tonight. I do hope we can come back again to this very important problem during the course of the present session and hear from all corners of the house so that we can demonstrate effectively, not only to the nation at large but also to ourselves, that co-operative federalism begins at this moment through co-operative parliamentarianism in this chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased about the present discussion, because it will allow us to become aware of the situation prevailing in Canada, since the need to make the necessary suggestions is being felt.
It is a comfort to know that the present debate, after many other occasions, is an indication at least that people are eager and willing to use their brains in order to find solutions to the problems now existing in Canada with regard to the relations between the two great races.
Mention was made of joint programs, of the action taken generally by the federal government in that field, as well as all the problems regarding federal-provincial relations.
This situation has been simmering for a long time.
Personalities from all political parties, from the federal and provincial governments, from the business world and universities regularly discuss it.
I should like to quote a few excerpts from various conferences showing the importance of the problem. Thus, on October 3 last, the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) mentioned, as reported in Le Devoir of October 3, 1963, the following:
The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine stated yesterday in Montreal that the time had come for the federal government to withdraw from provincial fields of jurisdiction, especially the social security field.
Lack of Consultation with Provinces
That was the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine speaking.
The leader of the Union Nationale party stated last June 16:
If Ottawa does not meet the demands of the younger generation, we will eventually be faced with separatism.
The premier of Quebec, the Hon. Jean Lesage, stated, as reported in the Globe and Mail on October 1, 1963:

On the question of joint federal-provincial programs Mr. Lesage said Quebec would always denounce federal incursions into fields reserved to the provinces by the British North America Act.

According to the November 4 issue of Le Devoir, Mr. Rene Levesque, minister of natural resources in the provincial government, also gave his views as follows:
Mr. Rene Levesque stated Saturday that Quebec will have to think of withdrawing from confederation if it is found impossible to have the two great nations of Canada live on equal terms in a federal system. Mr. Levesque added, when asked to deal with the taxation problem, that if Quebec does not succeed in making its opinion prevail at the next federal-provincial conference on taxation, there will be very few chances left to renegotiate the Canadian constitution.
According to La Presse of October 22, 1963, Mr. Gerard Levesque, a member of the provincial cabinet, said:
The old worn out trick of the "fait accompli" will be all the more intolerable as we shall be left with a choice between two equally unacceptable alternatives, abject subordination or total independence.
Le Droit of October 31, 1963, quotes Mr. Guy Rouleau, member of the House of Commons, as saying:
Unfortunately, French Canadians who travel outside of Quebec feel they are in a foreign land.
Mr. Speaker, those are statements which speak for themselves.
On June 29, 1963, Mr. Maurice Sauve said:
French Canadians do not feel at home outside of Quebec borders, and we feel also that the federal government is not truly our government.
Mr. Speaker, here is indeed abundant proof that we should stop and consider this national problem.
Today, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) spoke in favour of joint programs.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam even referred to the statement made by the premier of British Columbia to the effect that, under the equalization program, the province of Quebec had received $65 million more than it had contributed, and that it had everything to gain by remaining within confederation.

Lack of Consultation with Provinces
Mr. Speaker, I took the trouble to look up the most recent statistics and I find that it gets less than its contribution to joint programs. In fact, under our federal system, it gets much less than it contributes. All my figures are taken from statistics prepared by the federal government.
Let us take first of all the annual report of the Department of Forestry for 1962, that is the last one which is available.
Out of a total amount of $11 million paid by the federal government to the provinces in respect of forest inventories and reforestation, the province of Quebec receives absolutely nothing.
As for the grants to the provinces for forest fire protection and forest access road construction, the province of Quebec got $1,277,233, that is 18 per cent of the total amount of $8,823,680.
Again, the province of Quebec has not received a penny of the $4 million which the Department of Forestry has provided for air spraying operations.
My province has received nothing either of the $13 million paid out by the federal government for reforestation under forestry agreements. That is the situation within the Department of Forestry.
Let us come now to the report of the Farm Credit Corporation for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1962, the last report which is available. We find that only 1,869 mortgage loans amounting to $7,074,000 were granted in the province of Quebec out of 34,175 loans amounting to $217 million.
So, I say that the $65 million paid out to the province of Quebec under the equalization system is already more than offset by those various grants.
In fact, if we consider what has been received by some provinces much smaller than Quebec, we see for instance that Alberta borrowed $46 million, Saskatchewan $66 million, Manitoba $15 million, Ontario $65 million and, as I have already said, Quebec $7 million.
And the allotment by province of farm loans approved during the year ended March 31, 1962 indicates that out of 5,885 loans made in Canada, only 109 were made in the province of Quebec, that is 5 per cent; besides out of the total amount of loans, that is $68,574,000, Quebec received only $1,786,000, when loans made in Ontario amounted to $17 million, $5 million in Manitoba, $19 million in Saskatchewan and $18 million in Alberta.
A study of the same report reveals that out of 20 supervisors of credit working for the corporation, two are assigned to Quebec, five to Ontario, two to Manitoba, four to Saskatchewan and five to Alberta.

Of the 132 credit advisers in the country, four are in the province of Quebec, 25 in Ontario, 12 in Manitoba, 36 in Saskatchewan and 32 in Alberta.
Mr. Speaker, it is easy to understand why the former premier of Saskatchewan declares himself for joint programs, when in his province alone, there are 36 credit advisers of the Farm Credit Corporation, while there are only four in the province of Quebec.
In analysing the report entitled Technical and Vocational Education in Canada, published in English only, one sees that the federal government's share in the building of technical schools in the province of Quebec amounts to $25,714,000 while it amounts to $200,017,000 in Ontario. On the other hand, the province of Alberta, much smaller than Quebec, has benefited from a federal contribution totalling $37 million, as compared with $25 million contributed to Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, this does not apply only to this government, but rather to all the governments which succeeded one another over many years.
The annual report of the Department of Labour for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961 reveals that in the field of training given the unemployed, the federal government has largely contributed, and that out of a total of 10,774 there were 4,170 unemployed registered under this scheme in the province of Quebec. I believe that it is in this respect that the province of Quebec gets the most assistance because it has more unemployed than any other province in Canada.
On the other hand, for vocational training of the handicapped and for federal grants, we find that total payments amounted to $329,566 in 1961 and that nothing at all went to the province of Quebec.
As for training in primary industries and in domestic economy, the federal government paid out a total of $100,877.03 in grants and the province of Quebec received absolutely nothing.
Mr. Speaker, I see that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) is in his seat and I shall take this opportunity to discuss the annual report of the Canadian civil service commission for the year 1962. In so far as the grouping of the federal government employees by provinces is concerned, we find out that out of a total of 201,657 federal civil servants, the province of Quebec has only 31,952, that is about 15 per cent, while the province of Ontario has 87,369.
Those figures, Mr. Speaker, are thought provoking.
Mr. Speaker, if we take the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1962, we find that the payments made by

Canada to the provinces taking part in the hospital insurance scheme amounted to $678,533,000. I suggest the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam have a look at the statistics to see whether or not the province of Quebec wishes to keep on participating in joint programs.

And what amount do we get? That is the difference.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I submit that, in the province of Quebec, the hospitalization needs of the population are as great as in the other provinces. But, in our province, it often happens that sick people have to wait three, four and even five weeks to be admitted to the hospital because there are not enough beds.
But if the province of Quebec received its share of revenue, then it could build its own hospitals.
I think, however, that I could answer the question asked by the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
It happens that the province of Quebec, because of its mentality, its desire to grow according to circumstances that are peculiar

Now, if you look at the statement of federal payments for assistance to old people, the blind and the disabled-when the figures are favourable, they must be quoted also-you will find that out of $16 million, the province of Quebec gets $7,460,000, or almost half the total amount. I wish to give all the figures, those that are in our favour as well as those that are not.
By the same token, according to the federal-provincial agreement on unemployment insurance, the province of Quebec received in January, 1962, $2,957,000, out of a total of $10 million, that is to say approximately 30 per cent.
As far as the geographical distribution of full time jobs is concerned, on March 31, 1962, the province of Quebec had 358 such jobs out of a grand total of 5,213. Those figures are taken from the annual report of March 31, 1962, issued by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
If we look at the annual report for 1962, which we have just been given, I mean ARDA and not the Farm Credit Corporation Act, we will find in it highly significant figures.
Some of the loans are categorized according to provinces or to objectives, there are loans for buying new or second hand farming implements, loans for construction, repairs and alterations of houses and other farm buildings, loans for buying of cattle, and loans earmarked for various improvements. Out of a total of 72,621 loans, 3,244 loans have been granted to the province of Quebec, 13,508 loans to Ontario, 9,639 loans to Manitoba, 20,368 loans to Saskatchewan, (observe the difference with Quebec), 21,523 to Alberta.
If we express the total in dollars, we see that out of $118 million, Quebec has been granted $5 million, Ontario $23 million, Manitoba $15 million, Saskatchewan $31 million and Alberta $34 million.
I come now to the loans for the purchase of farm machinery. The province of Quebec got only 2,660 loans out of a total of 55,955, or $3,770,000 out of a total amount of $87 million.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, those figures are revealing.

We could keep on giving statistics of that kind. Let us have a look at the Post Office Department, for instance, and more particularly at the annual report for the year 1962. Under the following heading "Address-book, sales and distribution", one can see that out of a total of 9,739 post offices, 1,532 are located in the province of Quebec, 3,112 in Ontario, 1,329 in Alberta and 1,103 in Saskatchewan. Those are statistics that speak for themselves.
According to the 32nd annual report from the fisheries department, that is available in English only, mind you, total expenditures for all provinces in 1961-1962 reached $23,097,000. How much has been spent in the province of Quebec-$555,473 or 2 per cent of the total amount. In Ontario, the amount was $394,000, a little less than in Quebec, in British Columbia, $8,165,000; in New Brunswick, $2 million, that is four times that of the province of Quebec, and in Newfoundland, $4,600,000, which is almost ten times the amount spent in Quebec.
Now, let us take the report of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. There is a whole list of statistics; I will skip over some of them and will mention only the most important ones-development of roads leading to resources.
According to the 1962 report, Canada has spent $747,000 up to now for the province of Quebec out of a total of $34 million. No other Canadian province receives less than the province of Quebec. Newfoundland's share is $1,929,000, Prince Edward Island's, $3.5 million, and the province of Quebec gets


only $747,000, while Saskatchewan receives $4,457,000. Those are the figures, Mr. Speaker.
Let us look now at what we give. It will be interesting also to see what is given to the federal government in return for what is obtained.
I find, for instance, in the report of the Department of National Revenue, statements of the returns yielded under the Income Tax Act and the Estate Tax Act for the fiscal year April 1, 1961 to March 31, 1962. This is the last report that I could get in French. For the province of Quebec, the total is $925,722,000 out of a grand total of $3,588 million, that is 28 per cent in proportion to the population. In this case, we do pay our share.
If we look at the general income tax and the old age security tax under the heading "Direct payments by individuals", we find that the province of Quebec pays $130 million out of $557 million. Here again, we do pay our share. Under tax deductions at the source, we find that Quebec pays $339 million out of a total of $1,530 million for all Canada. We do pay our share.
With regard to the tax on the profits of crown corporations, the province of Quebec provides $405 million out of a grand total of $1,303 million. When it comes to paying, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec pays its share indeed.
Now, let us consider the excise tax: $410 million. If we refer to the table entitled: "Summary by provinces"-we have to look on the back of the report to find the French titles-we read the following:
Report of the Department of National Revenue, including summaries concerning the proceeds from customs and excise and other services, etc. ... for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1962.
Total receipts for import duties, sales tax, other taxes or excise taxes, various levies; total receipts for the province of Quebec $410 million; the province of Ontario, $497 million; plus the receipts from the regional offices, that is an additional amount of approximately $500 million and another sum of $50 million for the province of Quebec. We do more than our share in this field. And what does the province of Quebec receive in return?
When it comes to storing nuclear arms in Canada, over two thirds of the nuclear bases are located in the province of Quebec.
Such is, Mr. Speaker, the contribution of the province of Quebec. And we are told that we must maintain this co-operation. Well, I say we give but we do not receive proportionately to what we give.
They talk about the $65 million which we draw under the equalization plan, but this is offset by the contribution we make, as all

other provinces, to all joint plans, but from which we do not receive the share to which we are entitled.
It is not surprising there is agitation going on at the present time in the province of Quebec.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that we did our great part and that we are in a position to ask that this system be reconsidered, to ask that the province of Quebec be allowed to deal from now on with its own problems and find by itself solutions to them.
Time has come, Mr. Speaker, to set out exactly what the province of Quebec wishes and what it expects of a reconsidered constitution and a revalorized confederation.
First of all, and I think that the evidence which I presented at the beginning by quoting various excerpts of speeches given by ministers of the government of Quebec is conclusive on that point, the most important point on which we, Quebeckers, are insisting, is that the fiscal agreements must be reconsidered so as to restore to the province of Quebec its sources of revenues in order that it can develop in accordance with its own aspirations, its own culture and its own atmosphere, in short in accordance with the culture proper to French Canadians. That is the first point to consider.
We want to put an end to joint programs. We are convinced that if the province of Quebec is given back its own sources of revenues, so that we can levy ourselves taxes which we need for our own development in the province of Quebec, then we will settle the most important of the problems which are now facing confederation.
I should like to point out to the present government and to the Prime Minister in particular that the province of Quebec unanimously support the ultimatum given by its premier (Mr. Lesage) concerning the 25 per cent of corporation taxes, 25 per cent of personal income tax and 100 per cent of succession duties. Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Secretary of State and the hon. members of this house as well; I will only take five minutes to make my representations and draw the conclusions from the figures which I just mentioned.
The first means is the fiscal readjustment up to 100 per cent of our sources of income. And this has indeed been agreed to by the Prime Minister of Canada himself in a statement which he made in the house on December 17, 1962 in connection with the problem of bilingualism and biculturalism in this country. Here are his words:
It is now clear to all of us, I think, that Frenchspeaking Canadians are determined to become directors of their economic and cultural destiny in their own changed and changing society.
The Prime Minister himself was thus admitting that French Canadians are determined to become directors of their economic and cultural destiny in their own changed and changing society. We realize that and it is for this reason that we have given top priority to this plank of our platform. There is no way to save our culture if we do not control our income sources, if we do not control our economy, if we do not control our spending capabilities, so that our expenditures will be tailored to our own revenues and our own requirements. That is the first condition which will allow us to save our culture.
I heard a moment ago the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam tell us that the government would emerge weakened in its taxation policies if it gave up joint programs.
To this, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the government will never be weakened in its economic and fiscal system, or, rather, that it should not base its economic and fiscal policy solely on the levying of taxes from the people, it should base its economic and fiscal policy on something other than the taxes paid by the people, it must base it rather on the assets and the possibilities of development of the country, and not on the taxes it is able to collect.

Lack of Consultation with Provinces House of Commons certain policies and certain legislation which concerned the provinces, admittedly without having consulted with those provinces, before we were elected to form a government, which would be a new version of co-operative federalism. With all respect, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we can go quite so far as that in consultation.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), citing various ministerial delinquencies in this field of non-co-operation and non-consultation, mentioned specifically, among others, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud). He gave him, if I may use a vulgarism, quite a going over because in his field he had done nothing to consult with the provinces before the conference on fishery matters with all the provinces, which has been called to meet in January of 1964, I believe.
The Minister of Fisheries gave me the result of some inquiries he had made for me. I wish to point out that already in his relatively short period in office he has met with the ministers responsible for fisheries in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and he has received specific proposals from each of the ten provinces in connection with the January conference. I think that is a very good record in regard to consultation and a record which I think other ministers could, if not equal, at least approach.
I think we all agree that whatever may have been the practice in the past-by the past I am not thinking only of the last five or six years but the last 25 years-whatever may have been the record, whatever may have been the attitude of the federal governments in those years, the time has now come that we must consult with the provinces in what we now call co-operative federalism on every matter, not only those which are within their jurisdiction, in which case consultation must be obligatory and automatic, but also on all matters that are of direct concern to them.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to his own experience in this regard leading up to the resources conference. I think that was a desirable and effective initiative on his part and on the part of the former government, resulting in a very constructive conference which was responsible for the setting up of federal-provincial machinery which I agree should be a model for this kind of thing. This is not the first time this has been done, but it is the most recent occasion on which it has been done on such a large scale. As a matter of fact, I do not know whether it has been done previously in this way on such a large scale but I hope it will be the kind of

model we will follow in the future. If it is successful, as I am sure it will be, undoubtedly it will be a model for the future. There may well be that kind of a conference with a council emerging from it of federal-provincial ministers in other fields. Perhaps something will emerge from the forthcoming provincial-federal conference in this direction. I hope so, because that may be the direction along which we should proceed so far as consultation is concerned.
We were also criticized this morning and we have been criticized in the house very vigorously previously as a government, because we did not adopt the right courses in regard to consultation with the provinces on such matters as the municipal development fund, the contributory pensions plan and others. I mention only the two matters now, the municipal development fund, which is certainly within the jurisdiction of the federal government, and the contributory universal portable pension plan, which is also certainly within the jurisdiction of the federal government as the result of a constitutional amendment by agreement with the provinces that brought it within its jurisdiction.
Therefore, constitutionally, the federal government has the right to go ahead in these matters, and in putting forward proposals on behalf of our party when we were in opposition I think we were quite entitled- in fact, there was no other way of doing it- to put forward proposals for a municipal development fund and a contributory pensions plan. We have carried out one of these proposals and we intend to carry out the other. However, when we took on the responsibility of office we were then confronted with the problem which I suppose confronts any government in a situation of this kind, or certainly will in the future. That problem is whether the consultation which is required in respect of a matter in which the provinces express their direct interest and in which perhaps they share jurisdiction-they do in the case of the pension plan-should take place in advance of anything being brought into the house, on the general idea that we should secure their agreement in principle and perhaps even in detail with regard to the legislation before it is even introduced into the house in the form of a resolution. Or whether on the other hand we should consult with them on the basis of a resolution which has been introduced into the house and perhaps even legislation which has received second reading with the idea of changing that legislation in certain circumstances as a result of the consultation.

I think the latter course was the better in the cases I mentioned, and I think it will turn out in the future to be generally the preferable method of consultation, that is, to consult with provincial governments on the basis of a concrete proposal. You do, however, take the political risk in the event of the consultation, of withdrawing in some respects from your own proposals that you submit to them, and you will be accused of altering your proposals, of giving in to pressures and all the rest. But I do not think that is a very high price to pay if, as a result of the consultation and the changes you make, you then have a piece of legislation which will be acceptable not only to the federal parliament but also to the provincial legislatures.

I know hon. members of this house will reject, as I reject, any such dismal and disunited destiny for Canada. At the same time I realize, as hon. members realize, that in a federal state with a relatively few people spread across half a continent, a state which would be difficult to govern even if it were a unitary state, there are bound to be today as there have been in the past, pressures pulling us apart which must be counteracted by


stronger pressures to keep us together. Surely, the House of Commons can give a lead to the country in this regard. I think therefore, Mr. Speaker, there should be positive action emanating from this house, certainly from the government, which will achieve that purpose of keeping us together. We all have to admit frankly and honestly that when we talk about these matters while we are thinking not only of Quebec we do think primarily of Quebec, because it is Quebec and the French speaking Canadians who seem to have a sense of incompleteness, almost of grievance in the way confederation has worked out for them.
There is the problem of federalism. There is that of national unity. We have heard about them as linked and in some way complicated by the problem of the relations between English speaking and French speaking Canadians. Because the federal parliament and the federal government have an English speaking majority, although there are 11 French speaking members of the present government, they are inevitably regarded by some people in Quebec as somewhat remote from and perhaps at times almost even hostile to the aspirations of the French speaking people in Quebec. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) uttered what I thought were some very wise words this afternoon when he said that our efforts to discharge our responsibilities as a federal government are often interpreted as a threat of some kind to the special position, the special rights or privileges of Quebec as a province inside confederation.
When I listened to the hon. member for Lapointe this afternoon talking about the province of Quebec on the one hand, and the federal government, the federal parliament and the federal authorities on the other, as if these two things had to be separated, I thought to myself that the people of Quebec should also remember they are represented in this House of Commons and in the federal cabinet. While the provincial government in Quebec, of whatever party, will always have a special obligation and a special desire to protect the people of the province of Quebec, as any provincial government would have, let us not forget that that same desire to protect and advance the interests of the people of Quebec is shown by the Quebec members of this house and the Quebec members of the cabinet. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I reject this idea that there must be some inevitable conflict between Ottawa and Quebec.

speechtext: First, I should like to say that I never mentioned a conflict between the two governments. Would the Prime Minister admit that when each level of government has its own responsibilities and the means to take care of its own responsibilities, then the areas of conflict between both governments will be eliminated and there will be chance for complete understanding between both governments?

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
I am sorry if I misinterpreted what the hon. gentleman said. I did not mean to do so. Of course, I agree with him that the greater the clarification of responsibility-and that has been going on ever since 1867, sometimes successfully and sometimes unsuccessfully of the division of taxes, resources and other things-the more clarification that can be brought into these matters, the less likelihood there will be of trouble between the federal and provincial levels of government. I entirely agree with him on that.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is possible to believe sincerely and completely in a full and equal French speaking and English speaking partnership, as I think all members of this house do believe, without denying to the federal government enough authority and adequate resources to discharge the responsibilities imposed on it by the constitution, which are essential for the people of the nation and also for the well-being of the people in the provinces, as my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam pointed out this afternoon. I believe not only that the rights and privileges of the provinces inside confederation are a basic essential for co-operative federalism; I also believe that the federal government must have enough authority to do the job entrusted to it by the people of Canada. Surely these two things can and must be reconciled.
As far as I am concerned, adapting and perhaps misquoting the words used by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, who in turn was referring to the immortal words of a very great man, I do not feel that I was chosen to preside over the liquidation of the Canadian confederation. Because I believe in the Canadian nation inside that confederation, a nation strong and a nation united, just as I believe in full and accepted French speaking and English speaking partnership as the only possible foundation for strength and unity. To accuse any federal government of any party, as has been done, of being dangerously centralist merely because it seeks the legislative and financial resources to discharge its Canadian responsibilities is as wrong as it is to accuse a provincial government of being separatist because it seeks adequate revenues, an adequate revenue base, in
Lack of Consultation with Provinces order to discharge its own provincial responsibilities. Federal and provincial responsibilities need not, and should not, conflict in these matters, although it is very easy for that kind of conflict to develop unless there is good will, and understanding on both sides. It is also easy for conflict to develop through the action of extremists on either side, which action produces an extreme reaction on the other side. That is developing in our country today and it is our real danger. These two things must be reconciled, especially-I do not apologize for saying "especially"-in the province of Quebec, which is in so many ways not a province like the others. These things must and can be reconciled; but this reconciliation will not be easy to bring about. It has never been easy to bring about in any federal state, and it will not be easy in Canada either, where we have some very special difficulties facing us in this regard, not only in our relations between the races inside Canada, but also because of the relations between our own country and our neighbour, and indeed our relations inside the Atlantic community.
There is one special situation which arises here-I do not like to call it a problem, although it may be a problem; but it is also an opportunity-when we talk, as we do, about the two founding races. And I think we have a right to talk about the two founding races, because we must remember that there is not, and there is not ever likely to be, a Canadian race. This is especially true if we remember that not only did pioneers from England combine their efforts with pioneers from France to build up this country, but that today almost one quarter of our population is made up of Canadians whose origins are neither French nor English.
