speechtext: More.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: Someone says it is more than one quarter.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext: One third.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
Perhaps it is almost one third if you include the Irish. We sometimes call this one quarter or one third, perhaps inaccurately and rather loosely, "new Canadians". But they are new Canadians who have adopted one or the other of the two official languages in this country without giving up their own culture, their own customs and their own traditions which themselves are making an invaluable new contribution to the development of a new country. One of these people is reported to have said the other day before the royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism that he was worried about the use of the term "biculturalism", as if it divided all Canadians into two cultural

Lack of Consultation with Provinces groups, either French speaking or English speaking. This gentleman said there could be no second class citizens in this country, that you could not lump all these people not originally French speaking or English speaking into a group which was inferior in any way, or which felt inferior in any way, to other Canadians. Of course there can be no second class citizens of any kind in this country, whether through colour, race or creed. The only way in which we can maintain unity in Canada is by recognizing and glorying in our diversity. Canada is a country which must also be based on recognition and respect of equal rights.
Also very much in our minds as we approach the federal-provincial conference is the fact that there is a constitutional and financial duality to our federalism which must be understood. I have already touched on this. For instance, if the federal government at the request of the provinces, a request they have been making for a good many years-and in any federal system the provincial level of government or the state level of government is bound to make this kind of request-turns over more and more of the shared fields of taxation, or indeed all of them, to the provinces-or perhaps I should be more accurate and say to the provincial governments-then the federal government must either find the money which it has to have from some other source-and ultimately the Canadian taxpayer wherever he lives and in whatever province he may live is the single source-or it must ask the provinces to take over full responsibility for expenditure now undertaken, in whole or in part by the federal government. That, in a nutshell, is the fiscal problem. Again it is a problem of reconciliation between the federal and provincial levels of government. It is not going to be easy for any government in Ottawa to raise more money-and I am looking at the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon)-for its own increasing needs

and they are increasing-resulting in turn from the increasing demands made upon it by the people of Canada, the peoples of the provinces. It will be difficult to get the additional revenue required to meet these increases and often perfectly justifiable demands, and at the same time make larger money grants to the provinces, however justifiable the request for such grants may seem to the provinces. The federal treasury has exactly the same limitation as provincial treasuries. They are not self-renewing and each can only be replenished from the same source. There are those who argue that the transfer of both new funds and new responsibilities to the provinces would be the simplest and best course. I expect the hon. member for Lapointe would be among them.


But those who argue in this way sometimes ignore the character of our Canadian federalism. Their argument was met by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. There is a great disparity between riches, resources and, indeed, needs, in one province as opposed to another. As we all know, this disparity, which now exists and which is one of the facts of the present situation, has resulted in the concept of the equalization of economic opportunity and social benefits between Canadians in the various provinces as an obligation of the central government. That is now accepted, and it has been for some years-the obligation upon the central government to equalize opportunities and benefits by making the financial resources available in a calculated way to the provinces. We are committed to that on this side of the house as, I understand, all parties are now committed. To keep confederation strong, and to make national unity based on it stable, will require this recognition of the necessity of equalization, just as it requires continuous effort and willingness to adjust our basic constitutional structure to changing conditions.
It is obvious that the founders of confederation and those who drew up the British North America Act could not foresee the conditions which were to exist a century later. They were even uncertain as to political developments in their own time, and this uncertainty led a good many of them to prefer a unitary to a federal Canadian state. Fortunately the federal concept, with all the problems it involves and all the difficulties it created, prevailed. But federalism, if it is to be strong, must be flexible in the sense that it must adapt itself to change. We should not be afraid about that. This means constant re-examination and, when necessary, reshaping the constitutional act and the constitutional structure.
Today of course we all agree as to the necessity for such a re-examination and reshaping. As I have said more than once, and others have said this outside the House of Commons, while it may be a time for the re-examination and reshaping of the constitutional structure it is not a time for tearing down the building on the pretext of repairing and strengthening it. That would be as tragic for our future hopes as it is unnecessary for the solution of our present problems. All I have been trying to say means that there must be a close, continuous and co-operative association between the federal government and the provincial governments.
In the light of the amendment, as it has been moved, I am willing to admit that co-operation should be closer, perhaps, than it has been in the past. I agree, also, that there must be some permanent machinery set up to make this co-operation and this consultation more

Lack of Consultation with Provinces
effective in the future than it has been in the past. I cannot refrain from adding, when I say this, that consultation is a two way street in any federal system. While it is important that the federal government should consult the provinces on all matters which lie within their jurisdiction-and indeed it must do so; I believe, also, that the provinces should be consulted, too, on all matters in which they have a great and immediate interest. The federal government should, equally, be consulted by those provincial governments which give effect to far reaching social and economic plans which have a national significance. That is what I mean when I say consultation is a two way street. However, we must provide some continuing machinery for consultation and this is one of the items on the agenda of the conference.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to this question this morning and indicated that we had turned down a suggestion to this effect put forward by, as he described him, his young friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). But this proposal is not new. It has been put forward on several occasions in the past, but for one reason or another it was never carried into effect. If I may be forgiven for introducing a personal note, I can remember, back in the 'thirties when I was secretary to provincial conferences, asking some of the political leaders of that day why such a system could not be introduced. One of them was Mr. Bennett and the other was Mr. King. I made the same inquiry once of Mr. St. Laurent. The objection at that time, as it was given to me-I think it was valid in its day though its validity has, I think, diminished- was that if provincial representatives were permanently established in Ottawa to start continuous consultative machinery it would amount, almost, to diplomatic representation. The presence in Ottawa of such representatives would tend to accentuate the differences between the provinces and the federal government and, possibly, create a feeling of separation, increasing rather than lessening the differences between the two.
As I say, I think that argument has less validity at the present time than it might have had in those days, and I believe there is a great deal to be said for a provincial secretariat. I think the idea of such a secretariat as a liaison measure between conferences is not a new one. Nova Scotia suggested such an agency 25 years ago in its brief to the Rowell-Sirois commission. The idea was reviewed, later, by the Tremblay commission and in July, 1960, the premier of Quebec asked for a continuing secretariat in his brief to the federal-provincial conference of that year. I hope we shall be able to make progress with this idea at the forthcoming conference.

speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question? He mentioned a conversation he had with Mr. Bennett. Does he recall what year that was, because my understanding is that Mr. Bennett was in favour of such a liaison and that he came to this conclusion in 1935 shortly before he was defeated. I should like to know when Mr. Bennett made that statement.

maintopic: LACK OF CONSULTATION ON MATTERS UNDER PROVINCIAL JURISDICTION
speechtext:
I am not trying to hold Mr. Bennett down to a definite statement of policy as prime minister, but I remember asking him about this when we were going over on shipboard to the jubilee imperial conference in London. That would be in 1933 or 1934-[DOT] one of those years.
Anyway, there will have to be changes made, and one of those changes will have to be the development of some kind of machinery for continuing consultation between conferences. Another will be the holding of conferences more often, perhaps periodically, between the provincial and the federal governments.
Meanwhile, as consideration is being given to changes which may be required in our federal relationship, financial, constitutional, and economic, the federal government has to perform its task now, and within the limits of its jurisdiction now; and it has to do what is necessary for the security, welfare and prosperity of all Canadian citizens who, after all, are the same people whether under provincial or federal authority. In the discharge of this responsibility I repeat there must be no suggestion of federal policy being imposed on any province by Ottawa in matters which are in any way within provincial jurisdiction. The federal intention is to co-operate with the provinces in truly national policies which respect provincial rights, while protecting and advancing the interest and welfare of all the Canadian people. This, I submit, is the only way the problem of federalism and of English speaking and French speaking relations as an aspect of federalism can be solved. It is our most important domestic, political problem and it affects our very survival as a nation.
I do not underestimate, and I am sure no hon. member of the house could possibly underestimate, the difficulties in finding the right solution, but I do not wish either to exaggerate those difficulties. Nor as we face those difficulties should we allow our sense of proportion to be distorted by the noise from extremists on one side or the other. One hundred years ago the fathers of our country had no illusions about the task they were undertaking, but it did not daunt them and it did not defeat them. We are endeavouring to adjust harmoniously greater difficulties than have plunged other countries into all the horrors of civil war. We are striving to settle forever issues hardly less momentous than those that have rent the United States of America and are now exposing it to all the horrors of civil war. Have we not then great cause of thankfulness that we have found a better way for the solution of our troubles than that which has entailed in other countries such deplorable results?
The building of a strong united confederation, Mr. Speaker, on the foundation of the two basic races of Canada is still the better way. That is still the great Canadian challenge as it was in 1865, and I am sure that as our forefathers met this challenge in 1865 the people of Canada will be able to meet it in 1963.
We have had an amendment, Mr. Speaker, and we have had a subamendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). The subamendment deletes the words of the amendment and replaces them with the following:
That this house urges the government to carry out more fully the spirit of co-operative federalism and to consult with the provinces before announcing or undertaking programs which fall to any extent within provincial jurisdiction.
I have been talking now for quite a long time about what we can and should do as a government and as a parliament to carry out more fully the spirit of co-operative federalism and to consult more closely with the provinces on matters which fall within their jurisdiction. So the subamendment moved by the hon. member is clearly not a vote of want of confidence but an affirmation of a principle acceptable to the government.
I assume, Mr. Speaker, that when the hon. member who moved the subamendment talked about "programs which fall to any extent within provincial jurisdiction" he meant that if there is a program inside a joint field that is not a provincial field, and he was referring to exclusive provincial jurisdiction. We interpret the subamendment in that sense and I understand that is the interpretation which he himself gives to it. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we have no difficulty whatever and, indeed, we are very happy to support the subamendment. If the subamendment should be carried I shall then ask one of my colleagues, under standing order 56 (4)(e) to move that the Speaker do now leave the chair.

I am sure Your Honour will be taking advisement, for this indeed represents the greatest somersault in smartness that has ever been placed before the House of Commons on a motion. Now, sir, concerning the general views expressed by the Prime Minister about maintaining confederation, and as to making our contribution to assure it shall be preserved, that is our purpose and aim. That is the determination of members in all parties in this country.
The Prime Minister used a quotation from 1865. He did not say who it was who made the statement in question, but I seem to recall that those words were the words of Macdonald. Similar words were spoken by Macdonald, and at the time of the civil war in the United States Canada was engaged in nation building. The determination was made that this part of North America should remain under the British crown, and the means to achieve this were the establishment of a federal system.
The American system would not work in Canada. Weaknesses had been found in that system. Wherever matters were not specifically allocated to the central government in Washington, they became matters of legislation within the exclusive jurisdiction of the states.
As a result of the discussions led by Macdonald, and with the co-operation of Cartier, George Brown and others who participated, a plan was arrived at whereby we would assure the maintenance and preservation of the rights of the French, both in their language and in their religion, and would assure to

Lack of Consultation with Provinces them, not only for that generation but for all generations, the preservation of these rights. Educational rights also were left exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces. That was the plan; that was the objective; and I remember so well hearing in 1945 or 1946, when the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent said that those rights could be taken away by a simple vote of parliament. That was not then, is not now, nor ever was the position of the Conservative party. Those rights are unchanged and unchangeable, and must remain so, so long as this nation remains.

Now we have the strange and unusual position of the Prime Minister rising and stating that he pleads guilty on behalf of the government to the failure of the government to exercise that degree of consultation that it ought to have exercised, but having pleaded guilty to the fact that there has not been enough consultation he then, as a defensive measure, contends that the government will do better from now on if it is given another chance.
That is a most unusual attitude. To find a somewhat similar situation one almost has to go back to 1958, when the Secretary of State was given the credit of having been the father of the amendment that was produced at that time. I would like to have dealt with the particulars of that amendment but the time limitation prevents it. The question before us is that of consultation and the need of carrying out the spirit of co-operative federalism; that the government should consult the provinces before announcing or undertaking programs which fall wholly or partly within provincial jurisdiction.
The Prime Minister advances a new variety of consultation. What he says in effect is that the government will decide what is to be


done, will put it into legislative form and will then start to implement the legislation it has brought in, without consultation. If, however, the provinces object, then the legislative program will stop and consultation will take place. If the experience of the past few months is to be any criterion for the future, we know that changes will be made in accordance with the strength of the pressure exerted by the various provinces. In other words the new type of consultation suggested by the Prime Minister will bring about in this country disorder, disunity and disagreement that would only weaken confederation. It is indeed a policy of confusion, creating a climate in which confederation will be torn asunder. We have only to consider the experience we have had in connection with the Canada pension plan, which was brought in here with trumpets blaring and is now being withdrawn, held in suspension, because the provinces asserted that they had the right to be consulted. This is not consultation within the concept of confederation. Consultation should take place before the program is proceeded with.

Consultation after the event and after the federal government's decision can only bring about uncertainty, division and disunity. It will assure that a division exists between the federal government and the provinces that is the negation of the concept of confederation. The Prime Minister talks about abandoning joint programs. While he speaks of that, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) makes a speech outside the house. At the very time this is going on the government has plunged into areas of provincial jurisdiction under the municipal loans program. Then there is the question of the designated areas. First the government designates areas and, having designated them, when there is objection to them there is to be consultation thereafter.
The proposition advanced by the Prime Minister today is one that can only undermine confederation. He expressed himself as though he were Horatius at the bridge, standing as the guardian of the constitution and against the possible disintegration of confederation. Yet in the last few months, as a result of the failure of this government to carry out the principles of consultation as they ought to be carried out, more and more uncertainty has developed and there is more cleavage as between province and province, people and people and area and area than ever before in this country.

I need only read a quotation from the Montreal Star of November 7 in this connection to illustrate my point. I need quote only one small portion of it:
Left on the shelf.
Mr. Pearson must have the taste of ashes in his mouth. Also he must be cursing the bush-league flack who foisted that "Sixty days of decision" catch-phrase on him. He has had to announce the postponement until a new session, early next year of several pieces of major legislation promised in the speech from the throne last May.
Then it says this:
The explanation that the portable pension plan is being shelved because it would be "inappropriate" to go ahead with it before the federal-provincial conference later this month falls some way short of conviction. Why has the "inappropriateness" only now been discovered? Or is the government having second thoughts about the pension machinery-as it had earlier about its budget?
What has happened in consequence of this haphazard, uncertain procedure on the part of the federal government is that now when any legislation is introduced without consultation pressure groups in the various parts of the country, provincial pressure groups, commence to operate. The result is that whatever legislation is brought in is not in keeping with the demands of the people but rather because of the necessity of placating the provinces because of the failure of the federal government to do that which is essential to confederation, namely to co-operate and at the same time to discuss, consider and view it from the point of view of both provincial and federal governments when matters come within the jurisdiction of both.
Now, sir, an example of that is the royal commission set up on biculturalism. I wish I could discuss that this evening. I hope it succeeds. I would point out the warning I gave on February 4 last in this house when I said that if it were set up it would not solve anything. What do we find? We asked for a dominion-provincial conference on the question of amending the constitution and bringing the constitution back to Canada for the settling of disputes between the provinces and the dominion, as well as providing for those symbols of our unity that must be established if full nationhood is to be achieved.
They set up a royal commission. It is just like the cave of Adullam. Many of those who are appearing before the royal commission are separatists who have ideas that are not in keeping with our constitutional development. The result is we are going to have a hodge-podge of representations which have little relationship to the need of Canada. When the commission completes its work in one, two or three years from now, there will be no finality. Then a dominion-provincial conference will have to be called and the whole matter gone over again.

speechtext: At long last, Mr. Speaker, I am to have the opportunity of registering a grievance.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO CONTROL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext: At my expense.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO CONTROL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
I hoped to do so a week ago tonight, but the other grievance that was raised took all the time until ten o'clock. The grievance I wish to raise is the appalling increase in the price of sugar, and the fact that the government has taken no effective action to deal with the situation. There are indications that fantastic profits have been made out of the increase in the price of sugar, and so far the government has done nothing except to take refuge in their lack of constitutional authority.
The facts in connection with the price of sugar are known to every housewife in Canada. In the past 12 months the price of sugar to the consumer has doubled. There have been more than 90 changes in sugar prices in the past year. At the moment the price of sugar in Canada is at its highest peak since 1920, an all-time record for 43 years. This increased price of sugar has reached into the pocketbook of every housewife in Canada. It not only affects the sugar which the consumer buys for use in his own home, but it enters into the cost of processed foods, of fruit preserving, jams, jellies, soft drinks and a great many commodities. In every case, the burden of this increase in price falls on only one person: It falls upon the Canadian housewife.
We have endeavoured to raise this matter repeatedly ever since parliament reassembled. My friend, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather), raised this almost as soon as the house met on September 30. A week ago last Friday my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond (Mr. Prittie) sought to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the rising price of sugar. Frequently on orders of the day we have raised this question. The only answer we have been able to get from the government is that the rising cost of sugar in Canada is due to the rise in world prices.
I think we ought to take a look at this argument. We should recognize, first of all, that the figures given to us by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) this spring indicated there was no sugar shortage in Canada. If I recall correctly, he said that there were over 400 million pounds of sugar in Canada, which was slightly higher than the stockpile of sugar in Canada in April of the previous year. I am told that there is
Sugar Price Control
no shortage of sugar in Canada today, and that the stockpiles in Canada now are as high or higher than they were 12 months ago. The world price, therefore, had nothing to do with the sugar stockpiled in Canada and which had already been purchased.
If the sugar companies made, in addition to their regular profits, another five cents a pound-I think that is a very low estimate- it means that they pilfered another $20 million out of the purses of the housewives of Canada. A very fat profit has been made by somebody out of this very rapid increase in the price of sugar. The other fact which has to be kept in mind is that about 20 per cent of the sugar we consume in Canada is made from sugar beets produced in Canada, and certainly that part of the sugar supply is not affected by the world price.
Therefore, what do we find? We find that the sugar companies in Canada have been able to increase the price of beet sugar and have treated the price of beet sugar as though it were the price of imported sugar. The people buying sugar on the prairies close to the refineries in Winnipeg and Lethbridge have thus found that their sugar prices have gone up, even though that sugar is produced on the prairies. It is rather interesting to see that in the Chicago market beet sugar has been selling for $9.50 to $11.25, whereas beet sugar in Canada has been selling for $17.50 a hundred. One of the things which has disturbed a great many Canadians is that, while prices in Canada have risen to astronomical heights the price of sugar in the United States does not seem to have been affected by the rapid rise in the world price. For instance, in the northeastern states of the United States sugar is now selling for $13.45 to $13.55 a hundred pounds. At the same time a hundred pounds of cane sugar in the city of Montreal costs $18.65, in the city of Vancouver $16.60, and in the city of Toronto $18.55. It is very difficult, Mr. Speaker, to explain to the Canadian housewife in the city of Toronto why she should pay 97 cents today for a five-pound bag of sugar when United States newspapers carry advertisements, some of which I have here, advertising cane sugar for 49 cents for a five-pound bag. It is 97 cents in the city of Toronto; 49 cents for the same bag of sugar in the United States. This means that the Canadian housewife is paying almost twice as much as the housewife in the United States.
I think there are indications, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a great deal of profiteering by the sugar companies of Canada. I think they have taken advantage of the decline in the world sugar supply. I think they have made fabulous profits out of the large stocks of

Sugar Price Control
sugar that were in Canada long before the world price rose. The fact is that there is no sugar shortage in the world. It is true that the world surplus has been reduced but there is no shortage of sugar A statement has been issued by Mr. Arthur E. Beeby, executive vice president of Salada Foods Limited, and part of his statement is as follows:
The recent series of increases in sugar prices cannot be explained on the basis of supply and demand. There is no world sugar shortage. At the start of this year, there was a large surplus. At the end of this year, there will still be a surplus although a reduced one....
Reliable estimates for this year indicate that a 12-million ton carryover at the beginning of the 1962-63 season will be cut to 9 to 9.5 million tons by year-end. This certainly does not suggest a sugar glut but neither does it represent shortage_
Cane or beets for sugar are grown in more than seventy countries. It is obvious that orderly marketing of the resulting multi-million ton annual crops in the form of raw sugar calls for the buying and selling facilities of recognized commodity exchanges including future markets. The volume of future trading has been skyrocketing. On the London market, the 1963 volume was recently reported as $11.4 million. For the same period of last year, it was less than one quarter of this total, suggesting that the explanation of price pyrotechnics in sugar is to be found in this market performance.
As a major Canadian buyer of refined sugar, we are forced to the conclusion that the rising costs of this staple food item on world markets do not result from demand but from speculation.
I think, Mr. Speaker, those facts speak for themselves. We started the year with a surplus in the world of some 12 million tons of sugar. We shall probably finish this year with anywhere from between 9 and 9J million tons of sugar in the world. The surplus has been reduced but there is no shortage of sugar. The increase in the price of sugar has been due to speculation, due in part to a rumour that the U.S.S.R. might import large quantities of sugar this year. This has given rise to speculation in the sugar market. But the tragedy is that the Canadian housewife has been the victim of this speculation. She has had no protection whatsoever from this government. The best the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) was able to do was to tell the house that someone in the restrictive trade practices branch had telephoned Mr. Beeby and that Mr. Beeby was not claiming that there was any price fixing or anything improper going on.

maintopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO CONTROL PRICE INCREASE
speechtext:
Exactly. I was in the house when the minister made the statement and 1 was amazed that the minister made it. I was amazed at the minister having his officials telephone a man, a private citizen, to ask him to establish whether or not the Combines Investigation Act had been violated. That is the responsibility of the minister and his officials, not the responsibility of private citizens. That is exactly what this government has done. It has sat on the Combines Investigation Act and said to the Canadian people: "If you can prove there is something wrong we will do something about it". I am saying that it is the responsibility of this government to find out whether there is something wrong, and it is for them to do something about it.
What can the government do? The minister has made us one promise only. The restrictive trade practices branch will, he said, keep the matter under careful scrutiny and will take action under the combines investigation legislation if there is evidence of price fixing and collusion. Well, we expected it to do that. But I would point out, first of all, that this is too slow a process to do anything about the exploitation of the Canadian housewife. The investigation by his department and any legal action which might follow would take months, and probably years.
Even if the branch were successful in getting a conviction, this would not punish the sugar companies. Every hon. member knows the record of the sugar companies. The restrictive trade practices branch and the Department of Justice brought three of the largest sugar companies of Canada into court-the Atlantic Sugar Refineries Company, now called the Acadia-Atlantic Sugar Refineries Limited, the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company Limited and the St. Lawrence Sugar Refineries Limited. These three companies were brought into court and last January they pleaded guilty to a charge of making an illegal profit on 80,000 tons of sugar. In March they were fined $25,000 each or a total of $75,000. So there was a total fine of $75,000 on 80,000 tons of sugar which amounts to a

fine of less than $1 a ton-a fine of less than one twentieth of a cent a pound. I say to you now, Mr. Speaker, and to the house, that these companies did not pay a fine; they paid a licence to commit piracy on the housewives of Canada. Do not let the minister tell us that the combines investigation legislation is going to protect the housewife.
There are things which the government could have done. First, there is the matter of price control. The Minister of Justice says this is a provincial matter. I want the government to tell this house whether it has ever consulted the representatives of the provinces in order to find out whether the provinces would be prepared to agree to emergency legislation for price controls on sugar. Has the government ever asked the provinces whether they are prepared to delegate to the federal government authority to legislate in this field on a temporary basis or an emergency basis? After all, the provinces are also much concerned about the price of sugar. They each have authority to legislate concerning the price of sugar. The federal government has to give some leadership. What leadership have they given? Have they ever called the provinces together and said to them: You must be concerned, as we are, about the rising price of sugar. Are you prepared to delegate authority to us, or to act in concert so as to pass uniform legislation to control this situation?
There is another thing which the government could do. It could do what other countries are doing and go into the bulk purchasing of sugar. If necessary, after consulting with the provinces, the government could declare sugar refineries and sugar distribution facilities to be works for the general advantage of Canada. It could set up a sugar control board. It could sign the commonwealth sugar agreement under which countries in the commonwealth buy sugar in quantities under agreements extending over a period of time. This is why the people of Great Britain are getting cheaper sugar. This is why the American housewife is getting cheaper sugar. Here in Canada we are selling wheat under long term agreements. One of the reasons we are able to do so is because other countries buy our wheat knowing they can do so at an agreed price. There is nothing to prevent our buying sugar at an agreed price. At the present time many members of the commonwealth have signed the sugar agreement and are buying large quantities of sugar at agreed prices spread over a period of years. This would protect us from speculation in world sugar markets.
Has the government made any move to take action along these lines or to investigate the possibilities of such action? I say to the
Sugar Price Control
government: It is not too late now to look into the possibility of the bulk purchase of sugar and the setting up of a sugar control board. I say to the government: please do not take refuge again behind the lack of constitutional authority, because I am sure there is not a provincial government in Canada which would not co-operate with the present federal administration if it were prepared to do something immediately about stopping this profiteering in sugar. The provinces are just as concerned as we should be, because it is their citizens who are being exploited. They, too, are hearing the complaints of Canadian housewives. All they need is someone to give them a lead to attack this problem. Action in this matter has been delayed too long and I accuse the government of dilatoriness, of negligence and of dereliction of duty in failing to tackle it. I say the time has come when the government should cease sitting on its dignity and begin stepping on those who have been profiteering at the expense of the people of Canada.
I say to the government: the time has come to stop wringing your hands and to start ringing the changes on those who have been pilfering from the pockets of the Canadian people. I say to the government: If you continue to do nothing, the people of Canada will recognize that you lack the courage to face up to a critical situation. I say that if you do something, and do it promptly, you will earn the gratitude of the housewives of Canada.

Third, why are they higher in Canada than they are in the United States or in Britain? The answer to the first question is relatively simple. There has been a profound change in the world sugar market in the last couple of years. I might refer to the Cuban situation in this regard. In 1961, Cuba had an export surplus of more than 6 million tons. Last year it had declined to 5 million tons. This year, as a result of hurricane Flora, it is down to 3 million tons. Throughout eastern Europe sugar beet harvests have been very low indeed. These are the facts about the change in the world sugar situation.
The hon. member quoted some statistics in which he suggested there were great stocks

The council considered this estimate against the first forecast of supplies available for world destinations in 1964 and concluded that taking the year as a whole it would appear that requirements would again be considerably in excess of supplies. Thus the council envisaged a continuance in 1964 of the present tight supply-demand situation.

World sugar prices have recorded these fundamental changes and they have been very fundamental. On the London market, which is recognized as a world market, raw sugar prices were the equivalent of around 3 cents a pound about a year ago. As a matter of fact, for some years sugar prices have been drifting along at about the 3 cent level, as I have reason to know because I participated in some of the efforts to stabilize the world sugar market to prevent its collapse. This was a time when there were monumental supplies of sugar overhanging the world market, but these have tended to disappear recently.
Last May, when we had the first upward thrust in prices and the first decline in supplies, prices reached a peak of between 12 and 13 cents in London and then declined. As hon. members will recall, there was a very sharp reversal of the sugar market and prices came down, until in August they had dropped to between 5 and 6 cents. Then, after hurricane Flora they soared again to the peaks of last May where they are today.
I think hon. members will see that the proportionate rise in world prices of sugar is parallel to that of sugar prices in Canada. Indeed, the hon. gentleman quoted some sugar prices in Canada. I happened to be doing some shopping for my wife last Saturday and I made a special visit to the sugar counter in the chain store. There I noticed the changes that had been taking place. A ten pound bag

of sugar was over $2 and I can recall a year ago when it was down around 80 cents.
There can be no question about the rise or about the fact these prices are very closely paralleled in world markets. In fact, Mr. Speaker, in Canada the price of sugar is directly related to the world sugar price as reflected in the London market, and we in this case buy raw cane sugar on the basis of the London price.

rate, and to a British preferential tariff of 28 cents per cwt. The preference of $1 per cwt. is a contractual obligation to the British West Indies and other commonwealth countries.
Commonwealth exporters attach a very high value to their preferential position in our sugar market, and from our point of view it is the means by which we are assured adequate supplies to meet our requirements at all times. It would be open to us to suspend the British preferential rate of 28 cents, but that would simply amount to a reduction of a quarter to one third of a cent a pound, and would be comparatively meaningless in the present situation.
Another alternative is to pay a subsidy to consumers of sugar. We have looked at this proposition, and if we were to pay a subsidy of 5 cents a pound this would cost about $85 million annually. It will be evident that expenditures of this order must be appraised in relation to other pressing demands on the government and in terms of a realistic order of priorities and objectives. In other words, these two proposals, to remove the duty or to pay a subsidy, do not change the price of sugar to Canadians as a whole. They simply redistribute its costs.
The hon. gentleman spoke about price controls, and he knows, as well as I do, that we have no constitutional authority to impose price control. May I suggest to him in connection with his own suggestion, and to repeat again what I said, that I do not think I would be in favour of placing a price control upon sugar produced from beets in Canada alone. It seems to me if price controls were to be effective they would have to be effective on over-all prices, and this would be beyond our control. And if we put a price control on sugar in Canada, if we placed the price of sugar below world market prices we would not get supplies. I do not think this would be a feasible alternative, either, in connection with purchases of bulk sugar from abroad.
The government has been looking into the possibilities of a change in sugar policy of a more fundamental character. This is a problem of great complexity and is fraught with many uncertainties. It is clear from the experience of Britain and the United States that managed markets with respect to both imports and domestic production of sugar can lead to expensive commitments involving higher prices to consumers, and may in any event be inconsistent with our long term economic interests and our international trading relations.
Nevertheless, recent experience during this period of scarcity has not been satisfactory, particularly when we see sugar from Canada's

traditional suppliers being offered more cheaply to United States buyers than to Canadian buyers. I am sure hon. gentlemen will agree with me that, when we see sugar from commonwealth sources being pushed into the United States in order to establish a record for future import quotas, it is a little difficult for Canadians, who do not happen to have that sort of system to pay higher prices in consequence. The government is examining with an open mind the possibility of a change of policy.
The British and Canadian markets have constituted for many years the main outlets for commonwealth producers. A few years ago, in order to assist expansion of commonwealth production, Britain, through the commonwealth sugar agreement extended a guaranteed annual market at annually negotiated prices to the commonwealth producers. At the same time, in an article of the agreement, the commonwealth producers recorded their intent to give priority to the requirements of Canada through ordinary commercial channels, as I have described.
The commonwealth producers traditionally take advantage of the Canadian tariff preference margin in their sales to Canada by conceding about 15 cents out of the preferential dollar, taking the other 85 cents themselves, the 15 cents being for the purpose of ensuring that they get the business rather than some non-commonwealth suppliers. This margin of preference is sufficient to give them command over our market.
Commonwealth producers have begun to interest themselves in obtaining a significant share of the United States market, now that this market is open to all comers. For this purpose, commonwealth production is being expanded beyond consumption within the commonwealth preference area, and there are also new sources within the commonwealth, for example India, and these changing conditions may have an important bearing on a future Canadian policy on sugar.
As I indicated in my remarks to the house last May, the international sugar agreement does not provide the sort of protection to consumers I would like to see, and the government would like to see, and we are very much interested in examining a more effective form of agreement. We are also prepared to explore the future of Canada's relationship to commonwealth producers. We have been aware that similar thoughts have been in the minds of the commonwealth sugar exporters, from informal contacts made with them, and today we have received the following cablegram from the chairman of the commonwealth sugar exporters group:

Commonwealth sugar exporters now meeting in London are anxiously considering supply of commonwealth sugar to Canada and would welcome opportunity of discussing the practicability of offering annual quantities of commonwealth sugar to Canada for several years ahead at stable prices. We can assure you of adequate commonwealth supplies at all times to meet your requirements. Grateful you cable whether your government would welcome such broad proposals before the end of this year. Respects and regards.
We received another from Salisbury in Rhodesia:
Rhodesia sugar sales would welcome early opportunity of discussing with you possibility of long term agreement for supplying sugar to Canada with view to helping stabilize your internal price.
I intend to advise both the commonwealth exporters group and the Rhodesian producers that the Canadian government would be interested to consider with them any proposals they may wish to lay before us. So, in summing up, may I say there is no shortage of sugar in Canada. Stocks are higher than normal, imports are normal, and domestic production is rising. Prices in Canada have followed world market prices because they have been closely related to world market prices.
The government, however, is not satisfied the present arrangements give adequate protection for Canadian consumers, and will be discussing with commonwealth producers the possibility of long term contracts.
